en: First Act. Meditating upon whom— the bestower of boons and destroyer of obstacles in one's undertakings— the wise proceed.
Even in difficult undertakings, there is the destruction of obstacles; even in difficult,
even in extremely difficult tasks, they are effortless.
I bow to that elephant-faced one [Gaṇeśa] from whom [all things] proceed;
and [I shall provide] according to my intellect a commentary on the drama named Anargharāghava.
Viṣṇu, the son of Muktinātha Ārya, composes this Pañcikā.
This *Pañcikā* has been composed by me, a dull-witted person;
let it be diligently refined by the wise who are capable of discerning what has been said, what has been left unsaid, and what has been poorly expressed.
And its status as a *nāṭaka* (drama) is established by its having a well-known plot, a hero who is a noble and steadfast human being, and the predominance of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*).

Because it is endowed with the five junctures (*sandhi*), their constituent parts (*sandhyaṅga*), the intermediate junctures (*sandhyantara*), the subordinate parts (*upāṅga*), ornaments (*bhūṣaṇa*), banners (*patākā*), situational settings (*sthānaka*), interludes (*viṣkambha*), and so forth; as it has been said: "It possesses the nature of the junctures and their constituent parts, which consist of the stages of the development of the plot."
It is endowed with devices for introducing the plot, such as the *patākāsthānaka* and others.
"A Nāṭaka is defined as that which possesses the ornaments of the internal junctures (*sandhyantara-aṅga*).
Thus it is stated. In another text: "It should be joined with a divine or human hero who is wise and noble (*dhīrodātta*)."
"In which either the heroic (vīra) or the erotic (śṛṅgāra) is described as the primary [sentiment]," and so forth.
From the context, that work should be understood as a *nāṭaka*;
its plot is well-known because it is based on the *Rāmāyaṇa*.

As it has been said in the *Rāmāyaṇa* and other histories: "The subject matter is well-known from such sources. (3) And thus, Rāmabhadra possesses the quality of being a noble and steadfast hero (*dhīrodātta*).
Because he is endowed with qualities such as being a great being (mahāsattva) and so forth,
it has been said: "He is a great being, exceedingly profound, compassionate, and free from boastfulness."
"Steady,
with concealed egoism,
noble-minded, and firm in his vows"— thus [is he described] in the Mahāsattvata-kṛpa.
In the second act, by the passage beginning with "O Blessed One, this woman... (5), [the two qualities] are indicated therein— specifically,
the disregard for the cruelty inherent in Tāṭakā.
Since it was precisely her womanhood, which indicates her pitiable state, that was revealed, how could there be "great-souledness" [in the thought], "How shall I restrain him? (6)?
And compassion is indicated by the very remainder of the speech. In the fourth act:
"Rāma—(placing the letter upon his head) Dear Lakṣmaṇa..."
"Take Prajāvatī, who has been a fellow student in the service of our worship,
and go ahead"— by such words, his profundity, steadfastness, and the inability to tolerate delay as described in other texts are expressed.
In that regard,
by means of wearing [the manuscript] on the head, with enthusiasm as the root cause.
Even while dwelling in the forest— a source of suffering—
his profound depth was manifested as an unchanging composure; and since it was the women alone who caused delay during his departure, he spoke thus in her very presence.
Steadfastness consists in being free from doubt regarding the object to be performed by means of such application.
And [he exhibits] his inability to endure delay; and his firmness of resolve, since he does not accept the kingdom even at the request of Bharata.
In the fourth act.
Of the words of Rāmabhadra in the dialogue with the son of Jamadagni.
Because it contains the sense of "I" (ahaṅkāra), there is the state of having a hidden ego;
by the phrase "those summoned by others" (8) and so forth, the absence of boastfulness is also indicated. Being human is well known.
The predominance of the heroic sentiment (vīrarasa), however, belongs to that very [sentiment] itself.
Because it constitutes the meaning of the Great Saying (mahāvākya);
and because it is a descriptive account of the life of this [Lord], who descended for the sake of slaying Rāvaṇa, being of a sattvic nature and of the highest disposition.
And its objective support, O Rāma, is that [very same thing].
Because it has arisen as being inherent in that [substance]; thus,
"the substratum is the inherent cause of taste."
The Heroic (bhoja):
its stable emotion (sthāyibhāva) is enthusiasm;
it is characterized primarily by the perfection of the three powers—valor, majesty, and policy—as well as discipline, the three sovereign powers, allies, and so forth.
The *vibhāvas* are the profound expressions of the application of means such as conciliation (*sāma*) and so forth;
the *anubhāvas* are awakening, indignation, and the like.
The transitory mental states (sañcāribhāvas) and the two involuntary physical states (sāttvikas), namely perspiration and horripilation.
As it has been said: "The hero (vīra) is of a noble nature and consists of energy (utsāha)."
It is thus analyzed:
enthusiasm (*utsāha*), the perfection of being (*sattvasampatti*), and the occurrence of valor, generosity, and so forth, constitute prowess (*parākrama*).
Majesty consists of having an invincible and mature army; glory, fame, humility, and statesmanship constitute the power of lordship.
The power of mantras,
the possession of wealth, noble birth, and friendship— these and other such factors are the determinants (*vibhāva*) of the heroic sentiment (*vīra*),
as conceived by poets; they are further characterized by steadfastness, fortitude, and majesty.
Through heroic deeds, challenging speech, and the timely application of means such as conciliation (*sāma*), your expressive gestures (*anubhāva*) become profound with inner emotion;
they manifest as awakening, indignation, pride, ferocity, intoxication, and joy.
Mindfulness is steadfastness.
Longing, deliberation,
and envy are the transitory mental states (vyabhicāribhāvas); perspiration and horripilation are the sattvic [bodily] states.
"...arising from fatigue, passion, and so forth. (10) These factors—the excitants (*vibhāva*), and so on—manifest in various places [in other texts];
however, for fear of making this work too voluminous, they are not presented here. Even though...
The erotic, the pathetic, the furious, and other such rasas, as specified in their respective places, are clearly perceived there.

Nevertheless, upon a comprehensive examination of the introduction, the conclusion, the central theme, the narrative progression, and the fruit [of the work], it is the Hero alone who constitutes the meaning of the Great Sentence (mahāvākya).
However, for others,
the established position is that they possess the status of semblances (ābhāsa) and the quality of being "transferred" (sañcāritva), because they are subordinate to those [primary ones].

As it has been said: "The stable emotion (sthāyībhāva), nourished by the determinate excitants (vibhāvas) and other factors presented in poetry, becomes Rasa; this is the meaning of the poetic sentence."
It becomes clearly manifest. Even if it is interspersed at intervals by other entities, that which proceeds with a uniform nature from beginning to end will be the primary one.
When doubled at the beginning and end,
or when the first itself is joined with others, or when situated in the middle,
it becomes properly the semblance of a rasa; for rasas arise according to the requirements of the dramatic action.
"All shall indeed meet one another; whichever flavor is proclaimed first shall become the primary one. (11) Thus [it was said].
And the fruit of the hero’s activity consists of the attainment of fame, beauty, and wealth that transcend the world, as well as subjects such as the lord of the gods.
Dharma indeed consists in the form of protection; as it has been said: "Of a king endowed with qualities such as consecration..."
"The supreme duty is the protection of the subjects.
(12) Thus it is said.

Regarding the fact that dharma, when pursued for its own sake, results in the activity of a leader, Bharata states: "The task is the three-fold aim (trivarga); it is pure, and it has both single and multiple consequences. (13)
"Effect" means the fruit;
"the threefold group" refers to dharma, artha, and kāma.
And this [is stated] regarding the Ikṣvākus—
By the [sūtra] beginning with "likhitapathitā" (14),
and by the [sūtra] beginning with "prakṛṣṭakartṛbhiprāya" (15).
And it is indicated by the passage beginning with, "O Father, the pearl-jewel at the crest of the crown of ignorance" (16),
as well as by its being joined with the *sandhyā* [junctions] and so forth.
This will be demonstrated in those very respective places.
In that regard, there are sixty-four constituent parts (aṅgas), such as the introduction (upakṣepa) and others, belonging to the body of the drama, which consists of five junctures (sandhi).
The *sandhyantaras* are the *upāṅgas*, like the fingers on the hands and so forth;
whereas ornaments serve as embellishments for the body of the drama (*rūpaka*), which consists of both *aṅgas* and *upāṅgas*.

It is like bracelets and crowns [which are joined together]; as it has been said: "In order to convey the lack of looseness in the limbs at the joints of the face and other parts, twenty-one internal junctures (sandhyantara) should be employed here and there."
In this way, the body of the beauty of poetry, well-knit with its primary and secondary limbs,
should adorn the subject matter.
Clearly adorned with thirty-six ornaments. (17) Thus.
Now, the Sūtradhāra, intending to introduce the subject matter to be presented,

sets aside those preliminary elements of the *pūrvaraṅga*— even though they ought to be mentioned at the outset— since they consist for the most part of instrumental music; instead, he addresses that which is the principal among those elements:
It is endowed with an exposition of the objects of salutation,

contains auspicious words such as "Śrī," "Puṇḍarīka," and "Kambu," and is illuminated by the word "Candra" (Moon), which possesses a light as potent as that used for the moon's feast by the cakora bird.
He states the *nāndī*, which consists of two verses of twelve and twenty syllables respectively and brings about all auspiciousness, beginning with the words "niṣpratyūham" (verse 18).

Regarding the term "viramati" (concludes): it has been said—The introduction (*prastāvanā*) is declared to be the gateway (*tīrtha*) for the subject matter to be presented; at the opening of the introduction, an auspicious *nāndī* should be performed.
"Endowed with any one of these—benediction, salutation, or description of the subject matter;

generally marked by the name of the author; radiant with words of auspicious meaning; this [work] is excellent when it consists of eight, ten, or twelve verses. Or alternatively, regarding the word *pada*:

Because the word *pāda* is a synonym for *śloka*, these two verses consist of eight lines (*pada*). Furthermore, this [introductory verse] holds primacy, as it is said: "Even though there are many constituent parts of the preliminary rite (*pūrvaraṅga*) in a drama..."
"Nevertheless, the *nāndī* must necessarily be performed for the pacification of obstacles," because its necessity is understood from this statement of Bādarāyaṇa.
"Without obstacle," and so forth.

*Pratyūha* means an impediment (*vighna*); Amarasimha states: "An impediment, an interruption, an obstacle (*pratyūha*). The absence of obstacles is *niṣpratyūham*; [it is] an indeclinable (*avyayam*).

By the rule "vibhakti" (Pāṇini 2.1.6), an *avyayībhāva* compound is formed even in the absence of a referent; the meaning is "for the sake of the absence of obstacles. This is established by the rule "nāvyayībhāvāt" (Pāṇini 2.4.83), etc.
In the fourth [case], there is the substitution of *ambhāva*.
Some say it is an adverb (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*); in that case, the absence of obstacles would be intended only with respect to the act of worship (*upāsana*) present in the context.
But it is not for the sake of completing the work he has begun. "Bhagavat" means one who possesses *bhaga*;
*bhaga* consists of the six qualities. [As it is said: "Of complete sovereignty, valor..."
"Glory, beauty, knowledge, and detachment—these six are declared to be *bhaga*. (25) Thus it is stated by Parāśara. *Koka* refers to the bird separated from its mate at night;
*cakora* is the moonlight-drinker; [the compound refers to] the fulfillment of their mutual affection.

*Paṭū* means "capable"; *jyotiṣmantau* means "possessing excellent light," referring to the sun and moon. [The term refers to] those two eyes which possess [the sun and moon]. Otherwise, if there were a *karmadhāraya* compound of the words *paṭu* and *jyotis*, [it would be incorrect].

Otherwise, if the suffix *matup* were applied [after the compound], there would be a contradiction with the grammatical rule: "The suffixes *matup* and so forth do not occur when the meaning can be conveyed by a *bahuvrīhi* compound" (Pāṇini 5.2.120).
Alternatively, the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is added directly to the *karmadhāraya* itself, as in the example "possessor of all wealth" (*sarvadhanī*).

It is like [the compound] *sarvakeśī* and so forth; as stated by the author of the Bhāṣya: "The *bahuvrīhi* is formed from a coordinate (*samānādhikaraṇa*) compound, whereas the *karmadhāraya* is used occasionally for the sake of terms such as *sarvadhaṇa*. (27)

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), those compounds are included where the designation of the subordinate member (*upapada*) is natural as the primary meaning, whereas the designation of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) as the primary meaning causes distress to the learned.
For primary derivatives (kṛt), secondary derivatives (taddhita), and compounds (samāsa) are characterized by denotation.
[This applies] to those two who have become limbs of the Supreme Lord and who transcend all the senses, by means of their wandering.
By means of describing the worship of the two eyes consisting of the sun and moon— which benefit the world—
and by way of their wandering in the forest, [the text describes] Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, who are portions of the Blessed One, and for that very reason, transcendent, and who benefit the world.

The role of the narrator of the story is indicated. Since Lakṣmaṇa does not partake in the fruit [of the action] and is subordinate to Rāma, there is no room for the suspicion that he might be the hero (nāyaka);
as it has been said: "The primary [hero] is one who is connected with the fruit."
"That which is connected to that is considered a limb" (29).
He specifies those very [limbs] with the words beginning "by which," etc. A *palvala* is like a navel because it is the place where lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*) arise;

Amara states: "A *veśanta* and a *palvala* are small lakes. By means of half-awakening—that is, by partial blooming—the *śrī* (beauty/glorious lady) is *mugdhā* (charming/fresh), *madhurā* (sweet/dear), and *priyā* (beloved).
Regarding the word *yasya*: Amara states, "The words *mugdha*, *saumya*, and *nava* mean 'deluded' or 'foolish' (31)," and "the words *svādu* and *priya* mean 'sweet' or *madhura*" (32).

*ardhanidrāyitaḥ* means "acting as if half-asleep"; the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is used here in the active sense (*kartari*) from the denominative verb *ācāraky-aṅ*. In the context of grammatical derivation (*vṛtti*), the word *nidrā* refers to one who possesses sleep (*nidrāvat*).

Thus says Kaiyaṭa. Being of such a nature, he was made a rival (*sapatnīkṛta*)—that is, rendered similar—to the *kamboja*, the right-turning conch (*dakṣiṇāvarta-śaṅkha*); for the right [side] has the nature of the sun, while the left...
The sense is that, because they are of the nature of the moon, there is blossoming and closing; by this [statement],
it is shown that Sugrīva and Vibhīṣaṇa are respectively bold and timid, due to the presence of innate passion and being overwhelmed by the prowess of their elder brothers.
By the word "mukula," it is indicated that they have been established in the positions of Vālin and Rāvaṇa.
And it is also indicated by the word *sapatna*, which ends in the suffix *cvipratyaya* and conveys a meaning similar to that [of the original term]. //1//
Regarding "viramati" and so forth:

"viramati" means that at the end of a *mahākalpa*, that is, when the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) has concluded and the time for creation has arrived; the use of the *parasmaipada* ending is according to the rule "vyāṅparibhyo ramaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.83).

The navel is indeed a path, because it is the means for coming and going; in that very place is its one fixed abode or dwelling. Vāhaṭa has stated that the navel serves as the path: "In the fetus, a channel is attached at the navel and to the heart of the mother, by which he [is sustained]."
"He attains nourishment like a field from an irrigation channel" (35). Thus,
he— the Self-born, Brahmā— having become the artisan, the creator, at the very beginning of the three worlds, by virtue of being the originator of creation and so forth;
The meaning is that because there is no external object to be seen, there is entry within.
"At every moment" (*pratikṣaṇam*) means in each and every moment; this is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in a distributive sense (*vīpsā*) to denote "according to the object. Of what thing?
The locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the substratum (*ādhāra*), that is, the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*); why?
Because the effect has that as its support; for agency belongs only to one who possesses immediate cognition of the material cause and so forth.

As it has been said: "Agency consists in possessing the intention to act and the capacity for action toward an immediate cognition of the material cause" (36). "Arrangement" (*vyavasthiti*) means the configuration of parts;
[Brahmā] entered his belly in order to see what kind—that is, of what nature—it was. As it has been said:
In the *Liṅgapurāṇa*: "The Grandfather (Brahmā) again entered the belly of the Lord of Śrī,
searching for those very worlds situated within the womb."

"Padmasambhava" (37). The term "treasures of the world" (*jagannidhayaḥ*) contains within it the cause for his entry [into the world]. By this, [he is described] as the one who makes known the news of Sītā at the root of the destruction of all worlds caused by the end of the Rāma-avatāra resulting from separation from Sītā.

When [Hanumān] has desisted at the word of Sampāti, the entry of Hanumān into Laṅkā for the purpose of seeing Sītā, the difficult terrain, and so forth, is indicated. Because of its difficulty of access, Laṅkā is compared to a belly; even if one enters it by some means, [it remains a challenge].
Just as food and so forth undergo digestion within [the body], and not by way of exiting in their own form,
so too have the strength of the fortress and its specific protection been described. By this, there is a description of the actual state of affairs.
It has been done. //2//

At the conclusion of such a *nāndī*, there enters the *sūtradhāra* (the stage-manager), just like the [original] *sūtradhāra*; for it has been stated: "Another person, possessing the qualities and appearance of the *sūtradhāra*, enters in that same manner" (38); [he enters] with the *bhāratī* [style].
The ellipsis is "he resorts to the mode of performance" (*vṛttim āśrayati*). And it has been said: "At the end of the *nāndī*, the wise *sūtradhāra* enters for the sake of preparation..."

Indeed, the function of *raṅga* (the stage) should be joined with *bhāratī*. "Bhāratī is primarily the activity of speech in Sanskrit, based on human characters. Its four constituent parts (*aṅgas*) are as follows:
Bharata stated:

"The *āmukha* (prologue), the *prarocanā* (inducement), the *mukha* (opening), the *vīthī* (theatrical path), and the *prahasana* (farce). Regarding these, the *āmukha* is as follows: the *sūtradhāra* (stage director) speaks to the *naṭī* (actress) with propriety concerning his own task, while hinting at the subject matter to be presented.
"That which is called the *āmukha* (prologue) by means of a striking expression" (40).
This very same [element] receives another designation by way of a different form;
as it has been said: "The *āmukha* is twofold, distinguished as *sthāpanā* and *prastāvanā*; [the latter is performed] by the *sūtradhāra*..."
Conversing with actresses, stage assistants, and others.
Wherever one joins the introductory elements (āmukhāṅga) endowed with all the components of the prologue (vīthyaṅga),
one should introduce the subject matter at hand (prakṛta).
That is called *sthāpanā*. When joined with a small portion of the *āmukha*, it is considered *prastāvanā* (the prologue).

(41) In this regard, the *āmukha* should be employed in a composition (*prabandha*) rich in the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), whereas the *sthāpanā* is used in those consisting primarily of the comic, the loathsome, or the furious sentiments.

The distinction is that the *prastāvanā* (prologue) occurs when the work is characterized by heroism (*vīra*) and the marvelous (*adbhuta*); as it has been said: "In a composition where the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) is predominant, there should be the *āmukha* (introduction);
however, in one characterized by the comic (*hāsya*), the loathsome (*bībhatsa*), the furious (*raudra*), and so forth, the *sthāpanā* is considered appropriate."
"In a composition brilliant with the heroic (*vīra*) and the marvelous (*adbhuta*), the *prastāvanā* (prologue) is generally considered appropriate.
(42) Since this [work] consists primarily of the heroic and the marvelous, the *prastāvanā* alone is suitable; and that is as follows:

This is to be understood through such [deeds] as the victory over Paraśurāma, Bāli, and Rāvaṇa, the favor shown to Ahalyā, and the building of the bridge— [deeds] characterized by "heroic and wonderful undertakings" (vīrādbhutārambha)— which are praised by the audience.
In that context, the entry of the characters is called the *āmukha*, which is distinguished as a variety of the *prastāvanā*.
Intending to compose the limbs of the *Bhāratī* style, [the author] first,
for the purpose of propitiating the stage (*raṅgaprasādana*), offers praise to the local deity, the poet, the poem, the protagonist, and the subject matter.
He states the *prarocanā* (prologue), which is a limb of the *bhāratī* style and serves as the cause for attracting the audience, with the words "O, O! and so forth.
As it has been said: "In that context, it is the act of turning [the audience] toward [the performance]."
"Praising leads to persuasion" (44). Thus, although the sequence between the two aspects of persuasion has not been explicitly stated, [it follows as follows].
It is logical that the *prarocanā* (the prologue), which serves to attract the audience's attention, comes first, while the *āmukha* (the opening), which introduces the characters, follows.
The particle *bho bho* is used for addressing the members of the assembly.
[In the word] *lavaṇoda*, there is the substitution of *uda* [for *udaka*] according to the rule: "In a technical name (*saṃjñā*), *uda* is substituted for *udaka*" (Pāṇini 6.1.159).
The expression "velā-tamāla" (the Tamāla trees on the shore) is a statement regarding its being a sprout [of that shore];
here Kālidāsa says: "Dark with rows of forests of Tamāla and Tālī trees..."
"Velā shines forth" (46). Here, *kandala* means a sprout;
the expression "in the forest" (*vane*) is used because sprouts arise in a forest. By describing it as having the form of a *kandala*, he expresses its extreme delicacy.
*Tribhuvanamauli* refers to the place known as Puruṣottama; of that [place]...

Because it is situated upon Viṣṇu’s discus and thus not of the earth, it possesses the status of being the crest-jewel of the worlds (*bhuvanamaulitva*). It is metaphorically described as such because a jewel is typically found upon a crown (*mauli*); the specific mention of a "sapphire" (*nīlamaṇi*) is due to the fact that the Lord Puruṣottama was fashioned by Viśvakarman from a sapphire. As it has been said:
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "In that meritorious sanctuary, renowned as Puruṣottama,
[an image] made of sapphire was fashioned."
"The image is eternal"— by this he expresses its perpetual luminosity. Of Kamalā, that is, Lakṣmī.
He on whose [chest] leaf-sprouts—specific patterns made of musk—are fashioned through play upon his jar-like breasts;

or rather, who himself becomes like leaf-sprouts due to their firm embrace. This statement arises from the fact that leaf-sprouts appear upon the breasts, and by this, he expresses their eternal fragrance.

These three [qualities] are appropriate because of his divine body. The phrase "of the Supreme Person" (*puruṣottama*) is itself a praise of the deity of the place. *Upasthānīyāḥ* means "those who have approached"; it is derived in the sense of the agent by the rule *bhavyageya* (Pāṇini 3.4.68). *Kuśīlavaḥ* means an actor; [it is so called because] his conduct (*śīla*) is contemptible (*kutsita*).
"Vāti" means "goes," and thus it means "manifests. "Udvejitaḥ" means "agitated.

In another treatise: "Having entered [the stage], another person, possessing the qualities and appearance of the director (sūtradhāra), should indicate the subject matter, the seed (bīja), or the opening (mukha)."
"Or even a vessel" (49).
Following this as well, intending to indicate various matters such as the objects [mentioned] here and there, [the author] describes the oppression of the world perpetrated by Rāvaṇa.
It indicates a portion of the whole. The word "tat" (that) is used in the sense of a reason; that is to say, because he was made to feel agitation, therefore permission for practice is granted.
*Rasāḥ* refers to the aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*), such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and others. *Prekṣaṇaka* refers to a dramatic performance (*rūpaka*).
*Prayoga* means dramatic performance (*abhinaya*). Its permission (*anujñā*) is itself a favor (*anugraha*); this is the meaning.
Regarding the passage beginning with "nāṭya" and so forth: *nāṭya* (drama) is the imitation of the conduct of deities and other worldly beings.
As it has been said: "In this world, [drama] consists of the imitation of the deeds of deities, sages, kings, and householders."
"It is called *nāṭya*. (50) Thus, by the term *nāṭyaveda*, which refers to a single part, the whole— the Gāndharva [Veda], which is a subsidiary (*upaveda*) of the Sāmaveda— is indicated.
In the various forms of assumed dramatic representations (*āhāryābhinaya*), the *antevāsī*— meaning a disciple—
the locative case ending is not elided according to the rule *śayavāsavāsiṣvakālāt* (Pāṇini 6.3.18). By this [statement],
[the excellence] of Rāmabhadra [is indicated].
From Viśvāmitra, the acquisition of the *astraveda* (the science of missiles), which is a subsidiary (*upaveda*) of the *Atharvaveda*, is indicated as a single portion of the subject matter.

To the question, "What is your motive for propitiating us, who are terrified by other actors? he says: "Affection," and so forth. *Sadasyāḥ* means those who are worthy of the assembly (*sadasi sādhavaḥ*). [In this regard...]
The suffix *yat* [is used] in the sense of "good" (*sādhu*). "Beloved" (*priyā*) means desired (*iṣṭā*) and charming (*kāntā*). "By name" (*nāma*) indicates renown.
"That" (*tat*) refers to...

"My beloved! At this very moment, at this precise instant, I shall bring her—meaning, I will bring her. For this reason, the present tense (*laṭ*) is used for the future due to its proximity to the present. By this [statement], [the arrival] of Sītā, who was abducted by Rāvaṇa..."

Having thus established the *prarocanā* (the prologue) as a limb of the *bhāratī* style, he now intends to describe the *prayogātiśaya* (the dramatic excellence), which is a limb of the *mukha* (the opening) and is also known by the name *pātrapraveśaka* (the entrance of characters); and for that purpose:

"The *dhruvā* song delights and connects the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in a particular type of drama.

Now he describes the excellence of the application: "Ah! How is it so here? Vasiṣṭha is the son of Brahmā. By the word *ṛtvijā* (by the officiating priest), his status as one whose speech is not to be transgressed is indicated; for it is said that "an *ṛtvij* is called a performer of sacrifice."

Because Daśaratha is perceived as both proximate and present, and because the two words *etad* and *idam*, which respectively denote these two meanings and reside in the definition [of the *nirdeśya*], are used almost exclusively as indicators;
as it has been said: "By the introduction 'This is he' through the employment of the *sūtradhāra*..."

He conforms to worldly convention by thinking that it is improper to remain in the presence of two people who are conversing while he stands as a third; as it has been said: "I shall not be a third among two."
"O King Nanda, for what reason have I become a fool? (113).
"The subsequent action" refers to the preparation and so forth of the characters who are to enter immediately thereafter. "They both exit."
Because as long as the *sūtradhāra* has not exited, it is impossible for the characters who introduce the subject matter (*vastunirūpaka*) to enter;
as it has been said: "Having thus performed the prologue (*āmukha*), when the *sūtradhāra* has exited along with his attendants, [the play proceeds] with those introduced by him."
"One should elaborate the subject matter by means of *pātras* (characters). (114) Thus,

having defined the introduction (*āmukha*)— which takes the form of a *pātanikā* (a thematic lead)— for the subject matter intended to be expressed, he begins the elaboration of the subject matter (*vastuprapañcana*), which follows in due order, with the words "Then enters," and so forth.

In this regard—the subject matter (*vastu*) is of two kinds: that which is to be indicated (*sūcya*) and that which is not to be indicated (*asūcya*). That which is devoid of rasa is *sūcya*; that which possesses rasa is *asūcya*, and it is further of two kinds: the visible (*dṛśya*) and the audible (*śrāvya*). The former [the visible] occurs within the acts (*aṅka*).
It should be seen that the audible is also twofold, due to the distinction between self-revealed (*svagata*) and revealed-to-others (*prakāśa*).
Among these, the first is to be known by itself alone; the second, however, is twofold:
that which is revealed to all and that which is revealed to only some. Of these, the first...
That which is intended for the hearing of all those present on the stage is the first;
that which is intended for the hearing of only one person is the second, and that is of two kinds: *janānta* (within earshot) and *apavārita* (aside).

We shall explain the definition of these two in the very section on *sthāna*. As it has been said: "The subject matter (*vastu*) is twofold, divided into 'suggestible' (*sūcya*) and 'non-suggestible' (*asūcya*); the former is devoid of aesthetic flavor (*nīrasa*)."

Through the *viṣkambha*, *cūlikā*, *aṅkāsyaka*, *praveśaka*, and *aṅkāvatāraka*, the second [type of] *sūcya* (to be indicated) occurs, which consists of the weaving together of sentiments (*rasa*), emotions (*bhāva*), and so forth. That which is *asūcya* (not to be indicated) should be elaborated through acts (*aṅka*) involving five or six characters, or even two or three; that [latter] is of two kinds: the visible (*dṛśya*).

One should show what is to be heard at the beginning; the second [type of speech] is twofold, distinguished as "to oneself" (*svagata*) and "public" (*prakāśa*). That which is "to oneself" is to be known by oneself alone, whereas the public is of two kinds: that which is public to all, and...
And it is of two kinds: that which is of determinate manifestation and that which is of indeterminate manifestation.
It is all-illuminating and suitable for hearing by all who are present.

"The second [kind] is that which is appropriate for one person alone even among many; it is manifested in two ways as *janānta* (in the presence of others) and *apavārita* (aside). (115) Thus, the subject matter (*vastu*), divided by the distinction between what is indicated (*sūcya*) and what is not indicated (*asūcya*), is fivefold according to the distinctions of the seed (*bīja*) and so forth.

It is divided; as it has been said: "That entity called *prakṛti* is proclaimed to be fivefold: the seed (*bīja*), the drop (*bindu*), the banner (*patākā*), the small banner (*prakarī*), and also the effect (*kārya*). (116) Thus.
The activities of the protagonist and others are also divided into five types according to the differences in their stages.
As it has been said: "And there are five stages of the action, resulting from the activities of the protagonist and others:
inception (ārambha), effort (yatna), hope of attainment (prāptyāśā), certainty of attainment (niyatāpti), and the arrival of the fruit (phalāgama). (117)

Through the conjunction of these [stages] in their respective order, there are five junctures (*sandhi*) designated as "mouth" and so forth; as it has been said: "By the union of each individual stage with each of the *prakṛtis*, the junctures [arise]."

The objects of knowledge are comprised of sixty-four constituent parts: the introduction (mukha), the counter-introduction (pratimukha), the development (garbha), the deliberation (vimarśa), and the conclusion (upasaṃhṛti). These are known by the technical term "junctures" (sandhi).

The five sections are to be divided sequentially into sixty-four parts—namely, twelve, thirteen, twelve, thirteen, and fourteen—and these very divisions are called the *aṅgas*. As it has been said: "Having thus determined the beginning and the end..."

"And having divided that fivefold, one should further subdivide those parts designated as joints into pieces; the wise know that these shall constitute sixty-four limbs. (119) In this regard—the form consisting of the commencement and continuity of the seed—

The *mukhasandhi* (opening juncture) is indicated in the first two acts. Among its elements, the *bīja* (seed) is defined as follows: "The seed is a cause for an effect that has been briefly indicated; it is expanded in many ways, just as a sown seed, through the various stages of sprouting and so forth, leads to the fruit of a tree. And this [seed] is present here.

The seed (*bīja*) is Rāma’s inner-dawning enthusiasm, which acts as the means for accomplishing the intended purpose throughout the various stages— such as Vasiṣṭha’s instruction, Viśvāmitra’s arrival, the bestowal of divine weapons, and the reaching of Mithilā— just as one might consider the fruits themselves. The inception (*ārambha*), however, is merely the initial eagerness directed toward the attainment of the result.

"For the sake of further [increase]," he says. And that [passage] begins with "Rāma—(with joy)" (122) and ends with "How indeed will even that Viśvāmitra himself be attended upon by us? (123), [concluding]: "If this were so..."
By these two statements of the hero, namely "harsh as the end of an aeon" (kalpāntakarkaśa) and "the lover of the young Rohiṇī" (taruṇarohiṇīramaṇa).
It is indicated by that which conveys the activity appropriate to one's own enthusiasm. Through the continuity of these two,
the mutual connection of the twelve constituent parts (aṅgas), beginning with the introduction (upakṣepa), is called *sandhi* (junction).
As it has been said: "When the parts of a narrative are unified by virtue of the primary purpose, the connection of intermediate meanings is *sandhi*, by virtue of its nature as a joining. (126)
And he [is the one] who carries out, as the fulfiller, those various matters mentioned in the second-act *viṣkambhaka* which indicate the entire body of the narrative.
It reveals the seed (*bīja*) in the form of intense enthusiasm that has been projected;
as it is said: "The *mukha* [opening] is the emergence of the seed, from which various purposes and aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) arise. (127)

Thus [it is said]. Its constituent parts (aṅgas) are: the introduction (upakṣepa), the elaboration (parikara), the conclusion (parinyāsa), the seduction (vilobhana), the application (yukti), the attainment (prāpti), the resolution (samādhāna), the arrangement (vidhāna), and the contemplation (paribhāvanā).

"One should apply the twelve [elements] known as the 'causes of differentiation and division' (udbhedabhedakaraṇa). (128) Thus it is said: "Just as a man lacking a limb is not capable of undertaking an enterprise, so too a poem lacking its constituent parts is not fit for performance. (129)

Thus, these [elements] are to be adopted. Nor is there a rule that they must necessarily follow the primary plot (*pradhānetivṛtta*); as it is stated in the *Nāṭakaprakāśa*: "The *upakṣepa* and other [junctures] in compositions may be either principal (*ādhikārika*) or incidental (*prāsaṅgika*)."
"They should be employed according to the context" (130). Among these,
the sequence of the first three is intended, because they consist of successive stages.

It refers to those [dramas], and not to others, because in works such as the *Daśarūpaka* and others, the definition is applied even out of order, disregarding the sequence of enumeration, and because rasa, which is manifested through a specific arrangement, holds primacy.

"He enters while seated" means that for one who is already seated on the stage, "entry" refers to becoming visible to the sight of those seated [in the audience]. The word "this" (etad) refers to the verse beginning with "Madhu-Kaiṭabha" (131).
"Madhukaiṭabha," etc. "Medasaḥ" means of the fat, that is, of the oily essence of the flesh; "plavena" means by the reaching [of it]; the verbal root is "pluṅ gatau" (to go).
"Visram" means foul-smelling; as Amarasimha states: "visraṃ syādāmagandhi yat" (that which has the smell of raw meat is called visra).

For this very reason, there is the expression *medinī*; the suffix *-vin* [as prescribed] by the rule *asmāyāmedhāsrajo viniḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.121) does not apply here because of its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group. On this point, the *Vahni Purāṇa* states: "Those two Dānavas, having fought with him for a very long time..."

The two, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, who were difficult to subdue, were slain by Kṛṣṇa with arrows discharged from the Śārṅga bow. Then, the earth was fashioned by Brahmā from their flesh and fat; thus she is called Medinī.
"Then this earth shall regain its consciousness. If they consume it, then let them do so only after consecrating it; otherwise, [it would not be right].

Because spoiled meat is unfit for consumption; if they perfume it, it is only with their own glories, not with musk and such. If they perfume it with glories, then only with their own, not with those related to their father and so forth, in the absence of their own fame.
Because there is no stability in their sovereignty. If they endure [the throne], then they enjoy it for a long time;

if they enjoy it for a long time, then they are true lords of men (*narendra*). Otherwise, they are merely human beings, since even vassals and the like may come to enjoy power for only a short duration. Regarding the phrase "by means of glories":

By the use of the plural number, it is stated that "the king must achieve fame in many ways through acts such as giving and protecting. And regarding this [fame], it would be destroyed if he did not grant Rāmā to the suitor; therefore, Rāmabhadra—
The sense is that he "should be sent.
From this point until the conclusion of Viśvāmitra’s entrance,
the narrative is devoted to the dispatching of Rāmabhadra for the protection of the sacrifice.

Because the seed— consisting of Rāma’s resolve, which is capable of destroying all the rākṣasas through Vasiṣṭha’s instruction— has been indicated, this is the dramatic element named *upakṣepa* (the introduction).

As it has been said: "The sowing of the seed (*bījanyāsa*) is the *upakṣepa* (the introductory hint). Here, *nyāsa* means indication. [This refers to] the fact that Vasiṣṭha’s instruction is intended for the purpose of sending Rāmabhadra away.
"This matter will become clear in the passage: 'This object is seen through samādhi' (138). //14//

"Accompanied by reflection," and so forth. Reflection (*vimarśa*) arises because no reason is seen for sending a message when one has already been instructed many times; however, a smile occurs because that reason *is* seen.
He states that very reason: "By his command," and so forth. [The word] *apalitam*...
It is called *palitaṅkaraṇī* because gray hair (*palita*) is produced by it; the suffix *khyun* is applied here according to the rule beginning with "āḍhya" (Pāṇini 3.2.56).
For indeed, in one who is very old, gray hair arises at the base of the ears.
The meaning is that from childhood until this point, his command has not been transgressed.
For even now— in old age— he regards me, who am of excellent lineage and very young, as if I were a mere infant.

According to Amarasimha: "The word *rūpa* is used in the sense of praise" (140), and "the words *kukṣi*, *bhrūṇa*, and *arbhaka* denote the fetus" (141). The term *sarva* means both the known and the unknown;
he *anuśāsti*, meaning he instructs repeatedly. This is according to the rule beginning with "the roots *brū*, *śās*, etc. (142).
The root *śās* (to instruct) takes two objects. Therefore, "guru-pakṣapāta" means excessive partiality toward the teacher;
or rather, it means the partiality toward the teacher is greater [than that toward others]. //15//

What is being said? The meaning is that it is no wonder that a teacher is partial; this is the intended sense. He states that very point with the words beginning "of equal conduct" (*samānavṛtteḥ*). *Tārā* means the pupil (*kanīnikā*);
its *maitrī* (friendliness) is the affection of the eye.
This is what is meant by "pressing" (*premeti*).
He expresses this very point by way of an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle), beginning with the words "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) and so forth:
even though he is a common teacher, [he is such] in relation to you (*te* = *tvadviṣaye*), that is, in the sense of a general relationship.

The sixth [case]: *viśeṣadṛṣṭiḥ* means "one whose vision is distinguished," thus he is so called. Does the moon not cause joy (*āmodayati*) to what object? The meaning is that by its sound (*svara*), it causes everyone to rejoice (*sarvāmodaka*). It is like one's own entire property (*sarvasva*).

His "all-in-all" (sarvasva) is that which is the object of supreme love, and that, moreover, is the night-lotus (kumuda) alone; the sense is that this is because he is designated as the "friend of the night-lotus" (kumudabandhu).
This is an ornament (bhūṣaṇa) known as "reason" (hetu), specifically in the form of an "application of another matter" (arthāntaranyāsa).

As it has been said: "That is designated as the *hetu* (probans) which establishes the matter to be proven" (144); and: "That should be known as *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by another matter), wherein, having introduced a certain subject matter, there is the presentation of something else that is capable of establishing it."
"and from the object. (145) Thus [it is said]. 16.

He reveals his own devotion with the words "For me," and so forth. Thirst itself is the goad, because it acts as a restrainer. The function of the ear—the activity of perceiving sound—is the driver. The heart has the nature of an elephant, because it is difficult to restrain. [The mind...]
"Within the range of hearing" means that it has reached the ears. "Nothing remains" is the question posed by the tone of voice. *Kārikā* refers to a verse (*śloka*).
Keśava states: "The word *kārikā* may denote torture, but it is also used for a verse of exposition and for a composition. (146)

He causes [them] to remember, but he does not instruct; the remainder of the sentence is "through my mouth. The sense is that instruction (anuśāsana) consists of a form of persistence. By this, it is implied: "For kings employ gentle means."
The words of the elder Cāṇakya have been followed:

"the oblation" (hutam), and so forth. "The oblation" refers to the Vedic fire-sacrifice, such as the Vaiśvadeva and others; this term also includes the non-oblations and so on. As it has been said: "The oblation..."
They declare that *huta*, *ahuta*, *prahuta*, *prāśita*, and the offering of oblations (*balidāna*) constitute the *pākayajñas*. The oblation beginning with the *vaiśvadeva* is designated as *huta*;
that which is given [as a gift] is *ahuta*, while *prahuta*...

"O King of kings, that which is eaten by Brahmins, the offering into the fire of the vital breaths (*prāṇāgnihotra*), the consumption [of food], and the *balikarma*— that is, the offering of oblations (*balidāna*)— are proclaimed as *pākayajñas*. (147)" Thus, *iṣṭa* refers to the *agniṣṭoma* and other such sacrifices.
*Tapta* refers to the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other such penances;

*kuladharma* refers to the protection of subjects and so forth. The underlying sense is that the satisfaction of those who seek [one's help] alone serves as a substitute for the performance of all [other religious duties]. By this, [it is shown that...]
It is thus stated that Viśvāmitra, who seeks Rāma, must be made successful in his purpose. //17//
"From us," and so forth. "Mahattaraḥ" means the immutable one (*kūṭastha*).
"Rājanvatī" means possessed of a good king; according to the rule, "the suffix *matup* [is used] after *rājan* in the sense of 'good government' (*saurājya*)" (Pāṇini 8.2.14).

The word *nipātaḥ* [is used here]. According to Amarasimha: "In the sense of 'a land with a good king,' [the term] *rājanvān* [is used]" (149). *Svam* means "one's own. Regarding the phrase *arundhatīpatiḥ*:
by this, he expresses the perfection of his asceticism (*tapas*), because the duty of a householder has its root in the wife.

As it has been said: "The ritual acts of a householder, whether based on the Śruti or the Smṛti, have their root in his wife. (150) The word *api* is used here in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvanā*). *Svena* means by himself alone, even without being asked.

The meaning is "thus. Regarding the phrase "only this much": because it is so well known that one who seeks [instruction] must not be turned away, he intends the meaning of the verse to be something that need not be explicitly taught.
Since I have become a recipient of Vasiṣṭha’s grace, therefore—

The Sun is the best of lineages and the God is the best of deities; the sacrifices performed by me are faultless, and we are good kings. Because of our friendship, Indra holds himself in high esteem; such is the excellence of Indra’s self-regard.
The meaning is "born. Regarding "we" (*vayam*), by us (*asmābhiḥ*):
according to the rule *asmado dvayośca* (Pāṇini 1.2.59), because of the word *ca* ("and"), the plural is used even when there is only one [person]. //18//
"O royal sage," and so forth.
By the inclusion of the term "sage" (ṛṣi), he indicates that [the king] possesses knowledge of the true nature of dharma by his very nature; for this reason, the expression "innate" (sahaja) is used.

*Anubhāvaḥ* means power (*sāmarthyam*). *Mahimā* means excellence (*utkarṣaḥ*). *Gambhīraḥ* means unfathomable (*agādhaḥ*). "For fame" (*yaśase*) means for the purpose of accomplishing fame; the dative case is used according to the rule *kriyārthopapadasya* (Pāṇini 2.3.14). "You yourselves" (*yūyam eva*); [you] have set out.

This is the remainder [of the sense]. The meaning is that they are engaged in dharma by their own nature. The plural number in "you" (*yūyam*) is used for the sake of honor. [The Brahmins] are merely instructors and not instigators;
for Kṣatriyas lack the qualification for ritual action (*karma-adhikāra*) without instruction [from Brahmins]. (153)
This is the state.
Here he states an illustration: "it awakens," and so forth. In autumn, the *niśā* is the night;
by that [night] it is *niśāta*, meaning sharpened or rubbed. From that...

"Free from husks" means free from obscurations (*nirāvaraṇa*); the meaning is that even the moon of another season [is so]. "It causes to blossom" means it causes to open, becoming capable of its own function; likewise...
The meaning is that you too have engaged in this dharma entirely on your own, without being instructed by us or others. In this way,
through the praise of Vasiṣṭha, [the poet] addresses Daśaratha’s pride— which results in his disregard for Vasiṣṭha— by means of a pretext that is itself a praise of Vasiṣṭha.
He refutes this with the words "sa punar... and so forth. The word "punaḥ" (again/furthermore) expresses a distinction.
[The second type is] Parameṣṭhin = Brahmā, because [the latter] is his son. //19//

"Idam ityādi": "uditamuditam" means having joy arisen (*jātaharṣam*); the suffix *niṣṭhā* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). Alternatively, it means "repeatedly arisen"; in this case, the rule "nityavīpsayoḥ" is applied in the sense of continuity (*nityārthe*).
The word is repeated. "Constancy" (nityatā) means repetition, and that is a property of action. (156) *Iṣṭam* = sacrifice (*yāga*). The word *vā* has the sense of *eva* (only);
the construction is "only while performing" (*kurvann eva*). *Pūrtam* = a tank and so forth. *Udadhim*.

The story should be recalled that the ocean originated for the sons of Sagara, who had split the earth in search of Indra— the stealer of the sacrificial horse— after he had failed to perform the *pūrta* rites for his ancestors.
It is like a banner of good conduct.
The banner (*patākā*) is that which makes [the lineage] manifest, for she is renowned as the Bhāgīrathī because she belongs to Bhagīratha;
Bhagīratha, having performed austerities in order to deliver his kinsmen who had been consumed by the fire of Kapila, [brought her down].
The story that he brought the Gaṅgā [to earth] should be related here; the meaning is that all of this was achieved through his very power alone. //20//
Having described the merit in carrying out that command, he indicates the entry of Kauśika by way of demonstrating the fault in its non-performance.
By the words beginning with "O Kauśika," [it is implied] because it has been stated: "There is neither the entrance nor the exit of a character who has not been previously indicated.
Thus, [the object] did not serve for enjoyment; [it remained] only in the atmosphere.
Because it is established as such;
as it is said in the Rāmāyaṇa: "O Triśaṅku, go back! You have not made your abode in heaven; struck down by your guru’s curse, O fool, fall!"
"Headlong upon the earth. (158) The term "headlong" indicates the absence of enjoyment of the earth. //21//
*Pratīhāraḥ* means a doorkeeper (*dauvārikaḥ*); Amara states: "The two terms *dvāḥstha* and *pratīhāra* [both mean doorkeeper]. He stands at the door (*dvāram adhyāste*).
By the rule *adhi-śīṅ* (Pāṇini 1.4.46), the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) receives the technical designation of object (*karman*). The word *kim* is used in the sense of a question;
"Kauśika" [is the subject], with "has arrived" (*āgataḥ*) being the ellipsis. Here, a change in tone (*kāku-svara*) indicates respect.
He is to be known; for this very reason, there is a sense of urgency. "Having placed before him" means having honored him with offerings such as *arghya* and so forth;
according to Amara, "the word *puraskṛta* is used in the sense of 'honored,' 'assailed by an enemy,' or 'placed in front.'"
"Whoever [cuts] the kṣatra," and so forth.
*Ṭaṅka* is an iron tool for cutting stone. *Paritakṣya* means having made thin.
*Brāhmaṇam* means pertaining to a Brāhmaṇa.

The suffix *aṇ* [is applied] according to the rule *tasyedam* (Pāṇini 4.3.120). *Uccakāra* means "he carved" or "he manifested," the sense being that he fashioned her like a statue upon a stone. *Parorajobhiḥ* means "beyond the realm of passion" (*rajasaḥ*).
"By others" means by those who are characterized by *sattva*;
the inversion of the subordinate member [to the end] occurs because it belongs to the *rājadantādi* group,
and the augment *suṭ* is applied because it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* or *pāraskarādi* groups.
*Agādhaḥ* means "unfathomable" or "indefinable. *Gādhi* was the father of Viśvāmitra and a king; this is an epithet intended to manifest his status as a Kṣatriya.
The particle *api* is used here to express self-reproach caused by the arrival of a sage whose presence was previously considered impossible.

In the sense of "joy," because particles have multiple meanings: Vasiṣṭha honored King Viśvāmitra—who had arrived by the force of his hunting expedition along with his retinue—with various kinds of divine substances produced from the wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadhenu); at that time, the king...
"Even by me, the sovereign of the entire earth, that which is difficult to obtain has been acquired by this [man];
such is the power of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu)," he said, distinguishing her from himself.
He begged for everything he possessed; yet, even as he fought with Vasiṣṭha who still refused to give, he employed every divine weapon at his command.
"He was rendered powerless by the Brahma-staff; then,
realizing that the Brahmanic splendor is superior to the Kshatriya splendor,
he performed austerities for that purpose and became a Brahmarshi."
The story of the Rāmāyaṇa is to be sought here.

(22) (166) "Tell [me]!"—the ellipsis is "the lineage of Vasiṣṭha. The particle *kaccit* is used in the sense of knowing what is desired; Amara states: "The word *kaccit* is used in the expression of a wish. (167)

Since it has been stated, "One should ask a Brahmin about his welfare," this is an inquiry after his well-being. The meaning of the word "first" (*tāvat*) is: "The purpose of our coming shall be told later; for now, speak of your welfare. [This is] by means of the science of astrology (*jyotiṣā*).
"Together" [is said] because performing [the rite] in the presence of light is praised;
as it has been stated: "In the presence of the sun, fire, the guru, the moon, a lamp, water, and likewise other deities, [the performance] is commended."

"Recitation" (japaḥ). (169) Thus [it is said]. Regarding "one who has practiced dharma" (caritadharma), the form ending in *n* is established by the rule "dharmādanic kevalāt" (Pāṇini 5.4.124). Maitrāvaruṇi is Vasiṣṭha; [the suffix] *iñ* is used in the sense of offspring (*apatya*). (170) "From *dharma*, the suffix *anic* [is applied] when it stands alone.
The state of ending in *n* [is thus derived]. Maitrāvaruṇi = Vasiṣṭha; for the purpose of expressing offspring, [the suffix *iñ* is applied] after [a word ending in] *a*.
The long vowel [in *devatādvandve*] is due to [Pāṇini 6.3.26]: *devatādvandve ca*.
*Kulam* means "house. *Upatiṣṭhamāne* means "approaching," the sense being "for the purpose of requesting Rāma"; [the root is] *upa-sthā*.
In the phrase "devapūjā" and so forth, the suffix *śānac* is used in the sense of forming a connection (*saṅgatikaraṇe*).
In the word "cirantana," the suffix *ṭyu* is applied according to the rule "sāyaṃ ciram" and so forth.

"And there is the augment *tuṭ*. [The word] "especially skilled" (*viśeṣeṇa kuśalī*) means that you too have exerted yourself for the sake of Rāma’s request regarding the slaying of Rāvaṇa, which is your own intended goal; such is the sense.
Regarding "Viśvāmitra": the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule "before *mitra* when it refers to a seer" (*mitre carṣau*). [The word] "after a long time" (*cireṇa*).

The indeclinable [particle] *vartāmaha* is a word that resembles a case-ending (*vibhaktipratirūpaka*). "We exist" (*vartāmahe*) implies a dependence on mere existence; the meaning is that because the sight of Daśaratha is superior even to all our desires, we depend solely upon that. We have existed for a long time.
Thus [he speaks]. This indicates the weight of his anxiety, thinking, "When indeed shall we take Rāma away from Daśaratha and cause Rāvaṇa to be slain?
This section begins here and extends to the end of verse 177, "The story itself is coming to an end."
Because of the sending [of Hanumān] at Rāma’s request for the purpose of slaying the Rākṣasa, and because of the determination [to send him],
this is the dramatic element named *parikara*, which is clearer than even the stage of the introduction (*upakṣepa*) of the seed (*bīja*) in the form of Rāma’s resolve.
As it has been said: "The abundance of that [seed] is *parikriyā*. (178) Here, "of that" means of the seed;
"abundance" means its clarity (*sphuṭatva*).
"Sāvitra" means the offspring of Savitṛ. "You too" means [you who are] self-existent.
Even though they are capable [of doing otherwise], they thus conform to—meaning they desire—their role as protectors; the verbal root is *anu-rudh* in the sense of "desire" (*kāma*). (179)
"Namaḥ" and so forth: the radiance of the jewel on the crown itself is metaphorically described as moonlight; because it causes the sprouts to blossom, its "durddina" (cloudy day) is its raining.
"Durddina refers to a rainy day when the sky is covered by clouds, and also to a day of calamity," according to the *Vaijayantī* (180).
*Pratipadoktā* means "stated explicitly," as if spoken directly from the throat (*kaṇṭhoktā*), thus being clearly manifested.
The perfection of the two forelegs is prowess;
the meaning is that he has conquered all rival kings. By this, the excellence of his kṣatriya nature is described. The "moon-marks" on the hooves are those shaped like moons.
The places where [treasures] were deposited; by means of those, she was "danturā"—uneven with depressions and elevations—and she "sasṛje" (was created), meaning she was exceedingly well-formed.
The suffix *am* is applied according to the rule *kimettiṅavyayāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.11). By this, her perfection of Dharma is stated; by these two [verses], her blessedness is expressed. //23//

"From long ago," and so forth. "Stupidity" (*jāḍyam*) is that which is occasioned by false views or occasioned by the failure to see this [truth]. "In games," by means of "force" (*prasabham*), that is, by compulsion.
"Subhagambhāvuka" means one who was previously unfortunate but has become fortunate;
it refers to one whose arm has become capable of subjugation— the sense being that this play is innate to his arm.

In this context, the grammatical rule regarding the suffixes for feminine and masculine genders (*strīpuruṣasamādhi*) should be understood. Following the application of the *āḍhya*-type sūtras (Pāṇini 5.2.126), the suffix *khukañ* is applied by the rule "kartari bhuvaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.57).
Thus, *jaṅghālaḥ* means one whose legs possess speed; the suffix *lac* is applied here according to the rule "prāṇisthādātaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.2.96). *Tejaḥ* means majesty or prowess (*pratāpa*).
The meaning is that his prowess is unimpeded even throughout the three worlds;
for this very reason, [he is the cause] of the victory of Sutrāman, that is, Indra.

*sahakṛtvā* means *sahakṛtavān*. In the context of the section on past participles (*bhūtakālādhikāra*), the suffix *kvanip* is applied to the root *kṛ* by the rule *sahe ca*. [The compound] *manukule prasūtiḥ yasya* means "one whose birth is in the lineage of Manu."

This is a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* compound, as indicated by the rule "there is no [substitution] when there is elision of a verbal root before an *ārdhadhātuka* affix" (*Pāṇini* 6.4.24); as in the example: "He, who was devoted to dharma... (*Raghuvamśa* 1.1).
Thus it is said. //24//

"This," and so forth. It is a line—a row—showering a continuous stream of cool droplets of nectar; for the *Amara-kośa-śeṣa* states: "The word *rekhā* refers to a streak and a form. (190) *Paurastya* means that which exists in front (*puras*).

The rule "the suffix *tyak* is applied after [the words] *dakṣiṇa*, *apaśca*, and *puras*" (Pāṇini 4.2.98) means that the king spreads out the festive preparations (*kautuka*) like a cloud driven by the eastern wind; as it has been said: "The east winds are never fruitless. (192)
The *kalpalatā* (wish-fulfilling creeper) is indeed auspicious; by means of the knots of its sprouts— that is, its joints which are the points of origination—
there arises, through the rains, the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of sprout-production, owing to your partiality.
The meaning is that the prosperity of Daśaratha’s lineage has arisen.

This is the ornament known as *tulyatarka* (parallel reasoning), [which is here] by means of the two metaphors (*rūpaka*) called *meghalekhā* (line of clouds) and *kalpalatā* (wish-fulfilling creeper).
And because it describes the growth of the family—which is not directly perceptible—by means of a comparison with the Maruts;
as it has been said: "The description of an imperceptible object through metaphors or similes employed with a similar meaning is *tulyatarka*."
Thus addressed (193).
[In the phrase] "to the lord of men" (*narendrāya*), the status of recipient (*sampradāna*) is established by the rule *spṛher īpsitaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.36).
*Aikṣvākaḥ* means the offspring of Ikṣvāku.

The word *paṅktiratha* (Daśaratha) is derived from the rule *dāṇḍināya-naḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.11). Regarding the term *paṅkti*, it is established as denoting the number ten by the rule *paṅktiviṃśati-tyādi* (Pāṇini 5.1.59). Thus, *paṅktiratha* means "one whose chariot has ten [horses]."
Kṣīrasvāmin states that "a group of ten is called a *paṅkti*.
Since there is no mention of the lineage (*gotra*) for Kṣatriyas, only their names are mentioned; [the rule is] "the king [is designated] by the lineage of his domestic priest (*purohita*)."
"Let him choose [a name]," says Āpastamba. (198) Or rather, the mention of the lineage is simply "the descendant of Ikṣvāku"; [or] "the royal seers of kings. (199)
This is according to the statement of Āśvalāyana.
Regarding the word *bhavataḥ*, the dative case is used by the rule "namaḥ svasti" (Pāṇini 2.3.16).
*Praśrayaḥ* means humility (*vinaya*).

He asks about the reasons for their arrival with the words "I hope," and so forth. *Kāntāram* means a difficult path; as Amarasimha states: "A *kāntāra* is a path that is hard to traverse. Those whose tracks are like those of dogs...

"Those [are] beasts of prey (*śvāpada*); the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs according to the rule *śuno dantadaṃṣṭrākarṇakukṣivarāhapadapuccheṣu* (Pāṇini 6.1.142), and that which pertains to them is *śauvāpada*."

And by the rule "dvārādīnāṃ ca" (Pāṇini 7.3.4), the augment *ai* is applied; [this refers to] the stages of life (*āśramas*) of yogis whose internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) are firmly established in non-violence and other virtues.
Even lions and other such creatures are indeed peaceful;
as it is stated in the Pātañjala-bhāṣya, beginning with "One should be established in non-violence and the rest": "In his presence..."
"Abandonment of enmity occurs toward all living beings. (204) Thus, in the presence of one who has perfected non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), there is no room for suspicion regarding him.
He raises an objection, using the phrase "by an obstacle" (*pratyūhena*) and so forth, as a reason for the prevention of the destruction of the sacrifice;
the term "enjoyers of the sacrifice" (*makhabhujaḥ*) contains an implied reason regarding the transformation of the world.

"He is capable"; as he will say: "Others, out of anger toward the Lord of the Suras, were able to alter the world, and the seven ancient Brahmās, the fathers of the universe, were created. (206) Therefore, there is no need to fear any harassment from Rākṣasas on his part; thus, the request for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) serves as the reason [for his capability].
He raises an objection with the words "to do," etc.:
"to do" means as an object of action; "within" means in the heart; [it is] by way of being something to be done.
The meaning is: "Does it abide in the heart?

*Vasumatī-dakṣiṇaḥ* means one for whom the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of the wealth arising from that [earth]. It is called *saptatantuḥ* because it is extended by the seven meters, beginning with the *gāyatrī*.

Regarding this, there is the Aśvamedha sacrifice. In that context, although the status of the earth as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is understood from the sūtra beginning with "He gives the eastern direction to the Adhvaryu" (207), nevertheless, in that very same [text]:
In the supplementary passage [it says]: "Whatever wealth other than that of the earth and of men— [namely] that of non-Brahmins— is in the quarters..."

Because it has been stated, "He gives," the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists solely of wealth obtained from all directions. Nor should it be argued that "the universal monarch (*sārvabhauma*) should sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*)."
Thus, because the Aśvamedha pertains specifically to Kṣatriyas, Viśvāmitra lacks the qualification for it; [however,] "there is also qualification for a Brāhmaṇa in the Aśvamedha. (210)
Thus, because of the statement "it is not turbid," there is indeed eligibility;
or else,
[it refers to] the Sarvamedha sacrifice.
"Let the king who desires, 'May I become all this,' sacrifice for ten nights," so says Āpastamba, on account of the context.

The *sarvamedha* (all-sacrifice), and its fruit is liberation (*mokṣa*). In the passage, "He gives that together with the earth and the people," the earth itself is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); [this applies] here as well.
"The view of Hiraṇyakeśin is that even a Brāhmaṇa has the right [to perform this rite]," so says Āvilli.
The intention is: "I shall give even that land. The word "yat" means "for what reason"; the ellipsis is "you have arrived—what for? (tat kim?).
Since this sage is one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), he has no attachment to ritual action;
thus, [the opponent] raises an objection, using his own ripened merit as the reason, with the words "Or rather...
and so forth. And as for this state of being liberated while living:
The poet himself will say, "Even though he has realized the truth of Brahman" (214), and so forth.
Such [a person]— meaning one for whom your arrival is the fruit— is the reason (*hetu*).
It is either a transformation (*vivarta*) or a fruition (*pāka*) of the ascetic merits of the Raghu dynasty;
since the root *vas* here has the sense of "existence," the suffix *tumun* is not applied to the root *kṛ* by the rule *śakadhṛṣajñāglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhāstārthāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.65).
Regarding the rule *tumunṇvulau* (Pāṇini 3.3.10): although the action of "doing" (*kartum*), expressed by the verbal noun ending in *tumun* from the root *saptatantu*,

functions as the object (*karman*) with respect to the instrumental action of weaving, it [does not function as such] with respect to the action of dwelling (*nivāsakriyā*), which is expressed by the verb *vasati*.

The accusative case does not occur because of the [agent's] status as the agent (kartṛtva); for between the two actions expressed by the noun and the verb, the action expressed by the verb alone possesses primacy due to its being that which is yet to be accomplished (sādhya),
and the case-ending arises in accordance with that [primary action], while the agent is already expressed by the verbal suffix (tiṅ).
Since a third case-ending is absent, the nominative is employed by the rule "prātipadikārtha" (Pāṇini 2.3.46) in order to establish the status of the word as a nominal base. //25//

He addresses the objection that "protecting the sacrifice" is merely a royal prerogative—even though it is required—by stating "he brings forth," and so on. He brings forth even Indra and the other gods by the mere courtyard of his house; he is a "householder" (kuṭumbin), meaning one who possesses a group of dependents to be nourished, and he "brings them forth" (janayati), meaning he has created them.
While [Indra and others exist], Indra and the rest are lords only over the courtyard of their own homes; the sense is that You alone are the Lord of those worlds.

*Śruti* means sound; *na vāstavī* means devoid of objective reality (*arthaśūnyā*). *Pratibhayam* means fear arising from something adverse. The suffix *loṭ* in *astu* is used in the sense of the time having arrived (according to Pāṇini 3.3.163); the meaning is: "from where has the time for fear arrived?"
The sense is: "Since there is no enemy at all, how can there be fear caused by him? The word "hero" (*vīra*) is an epithet containing a reason [for his fearlessness]. //26//

He states that you are not only a benefactor of Indra and others, but also of Viṣṇu as well—beginning with the words "Datta" and so forth. "Datta" means one by whom the gift (*dakṣiṇā*) of fearlessness has been given; thus he is so described.
In the *Itihāsasamuccaya*, when Nahuṣa asks, "What is the gift? [the answer follows].

"Charity, however, is the gift of fearlessness"—this is the reply of Dharmarāja; the meaning is that the gift of fearlessness alone is true charity. For this very reason, he is called "the marvelous one," and "Manuṣya Devatrāta."

And that aforementioned abundance (*saṃbhāra*)—meaning prosperity or strength—of his two arms; by means of that, she is profound (*gambhīrā*), meaning unassailable. *Tribhuvanam* refers to the three worlds (*trilokī*).
In order to provide protection for the people as their refuge;
[this is expressed] by the rule beginning with "kriyārthopapadasya" (Pāṇini 2.3.14).

The fourth [explanation]: "relaxed" (*śithilīkṛta*). Previously, before your appearance, he was girded for the protection of the world; now, because the burden has been placed upon you, his effort is relaxed—this is the meaning. For this very reason, the suffix *cv* is employed. (222)
Due to the absence of the burden of internal anxiety, a joy was born; from that joy,
by being filled with breaths that were cool as frost and naturally fragrant like the wind of exhalation, his vital strength (*prāṇa*) became lofty.
In which action there was a bed or couch called Śeṣa;
for the serpent, air is food, and that [air] became undrinkable because it was hot with anxiety, whereby Śeṣa became emaciated; now, however, he is pot-bellied because of eating delicacies.
This is the meaning: those whose fillers (*āpūraṇāḥ*)—that is, their fillers—are the very winds of breath (*śvāsānilāḥ*);
because they are filled by a homogeneous [wind] called *prāṇa*, or because of the swelling caused by them, the loftiness (*tuṅgatvam*) of the couch (*talpasya*) [is established].

It is as if born from a bellows; for this very reason, there is the pleasure of sleep. "Nidrāyate" means he acts like one who possesses sleep; thus, "in the context of its function, the word *nidrā* refers to that which possesses sleep."

Kaiyaṭa [states]: (223) [The suffix] *kyaṣ* is applied because [the word *bhāra*] belongs to the *lohitādi* group. (224) His resolution is that one whose burden has been laid down becomes possessed of pleasant sleep; for it is said: "The term *prāṇa* [is used] for the *praṇava*, for the individual soul (*jīva*), for life, and for the Supreme Self."
"In the sense-faculties, in the divisions of the wind, and also in strength and the inner controller," thus says the *Vaijayantī*. (225) 27.
*Vailakṣyam* is shame, arising from self-praise. Regarding the term *abhyamittrīṇaḥ*, it means "one who goes against enemies"; this is derived according to Pāṇini 5.2.17 (*abhyamittrāc cha ca*).
From the word *ca* (and), [the suffix] *kha* is applied.

*Śunāsīra* is Indra. *Nāsīra* is the vanguard of an army; one who fills that [vanguard] means one who is not an instigator. *Uddhṛta* means extracted, but not made with an arrow. *Alīka* means untrue. *Āpyāyayati* means to please.
"Sotprāśam" means with an underlying intention;
that is, it was said again as a mere falsehood.

He speaks by way of praising Daśaratha, beginning with "trailokya... and so forth. *Lagnaka* means a guarantor (*pratibhū*); as Amarasimha states: "The *lagnakas* are guarantors" (2.8.227); that is to say, one who gives [as security].

"By Vīra" is an epithet containing the reason for his being forgotten; the cause of his being forgotten is that the burden of battle was placed upon him. "Tat" (that) is used in the sense of something well-known.
Because it dissolves after that [moment], it is the "ornament for a mere moment" (*muhūrtamaṇḍanatva*).
"Samphulla" means blossomed or fully developed; this is a *nipāta* (irregular form) according to the rule:
"The addition of *utphulla* and *samphulla* [is prescribed]. (Pāṇini 6.1.228).
*sarvāṅgīṇaḥ* means pervading all limbs; [the suffix] *kha* is applied according to the rule "tatsarvādeḥ" (Pāṇini 5.2.7).
*viluptaḥ* means covered. *Vyūhaḥ* means a collection.
[This is so] because of the absence of practice with the bow.
And there is corpulence resulting from the consumption of sacrificial oblations such as *puroḍāśa* without restraint; the question is: "How does he exist?"—whether with ease or with difficulty.
This is the ornament known as *prāpti*.
This is inferred from the fact that Indra’s body became bloated due to the lack of exercise with his bow, resulting from his assistance in Daśaratha’s ritual performance;
as it has been said: "From the knowledge of one part, there is the attainment [of the whole] through the application of the remainder. (230) //28//
Regarding this, he states as a witness: "Mahārāja," and so forth. "Kāśyapa" refers to Indra;
the meaning is that it is the world itself that is inferior, not his capacity. The phrase "just as he said" implies "in that very manner."
"Upon you," and so forth.
Sharing half the seat is established by tradition (*kulasiddha*); regarding this, Kālidāsa says—"half the seat."
"He stood at the breaking of the lineage" (gotrabhido 'dhitasthau).
Here, because the word *ardha* signifies an equal division, [the rule] "the neuter form is used for *ardha*" (*ardhaṃ napuṃsakam*) applies.
In a compound, the word *ardha* takes the first position.
*Sambhṛtamatsaraḥ* means one who has developed hatred for the praise of Daśaratha’s virtues; Amarasimha states: "Envy (*matsara*) is hatred of another's excellence" (2.33). *Kṛtī* means skillful.
The meaning is that he acted with tears arising from the experience of joy at the very concealment of his stinginess; [he mentions] the "right arm" because of its role as a servant.
Because of being situated in a low position;
horripilation arises from hearing praise of oneself; and tears arise from piercing—this is expressed by the agentive suffix in the word "abhinayati" (he acts out).
It should be understood that piercing (vedha) is also performed by the effort of the senses. Even when one eye is impaired, tears arise in the others as well;
thus, the plural "by the eyes" (nayanaiḥ) is used.
The sense is that the gods, not recognizing this cause, perceived it as being caused by bliss. //29//
"Anupraviṣṭaḥ" means "favorable.
Indra says "to him," etc., because he is capable by his own nature.
"Tiṣṭheta" means "would he dare to manifest his desire for battle through audacity"? The *ātmanepada* ending is used according to Pāṇini 1.3.23, *prakāśanastheyākhyayośca*.
The status of the recipient (*sampradāna*) is established by the rule *ślāghahuṅsthāśapām* (Pāṇini 1.4.34). The term *jambhārayaḥ* is used to highlight his valor.
*Bahirniryadbhiḥ* means "issuing forth" or "coming out. *Rajyadbhiḥ* means "reddened";
[this is derived from the root *rañj*] according to the rule *kuṣirajoḥ prācāṃ śyan* (Pāṇini 3.1.90).
And [the rule] *parasmaipadañ ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.98).
Merely by the look of his eyes, which are red with rage, his enemies flee as if struck by the fiery weapon (*āgneyāstra*); how then could there even be a battle?
The meaning of the word "also" (api) is as follows: //30//
The touching of his arm was out of great respect; "O royal sage, disciple of Vasiṣṭha"—thus were his excellence in human and divine qualities described. Your assistance to Indra is not a new thing.

He says "because it has come down through family lineage," beginning with the words "he became," etc.: "If Indra has become one whose prosperity is free from obstacles, then [it is] by the shade of your arm. This is the [meaning].
What kind of praise is yours that it is "new"?
It means it is not new at all.
He says this very thing in the passage beginning with "of the Ikṣvākus," etc. [Of the Ikṣvākus...]

[This is] for those belonging to your lineage; there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix denoting "king" (*rājapratyaya*). The protection of livestock—consisting of the form of a female crocodile (*makarī*) situated within the leaf-designs on the cheeks of celestial women—is their livelihood (*vṛtti*), that is, their means of subsistence; it is as if fashioned by one who has both written and recited [the art].
By the use of the plural form "of the Ikṣvākus," he refers specifically to Rāma;
by this, it is indicated that [Viṣṇu] has descended for this very purpose. The compound "pāśupālyaṃ makarīṣu" (cattle-tending among the female crocodiles) is a locative tatpuruṣa compound. //31//

The state of being a marvelous treasure [is established] because of his being the creator of the world. The phrase "what need is there to mention [his] manly power? (pauruṣeṇa kim uta) implies that this is so even through the exchange of questions and answers; such is the meaning of the word "even" (api).
He states that very point with the passage ending in "kamalabhūḥ" (238).
Triśaṅku was a king of the Ikṣvāku lineage; that by which he is celebrated through a narrative is so described.
And that is well known in the Rāmāyaṇa.
"Pāradṛśvānaḥ" means those who have seen the further shore (*pāradarśinaḥ*), from the root *dṛś*.
*kvanip* (240);
*kila* means "as is well known. Regarding *trāsa* and so forth: *smeram* means "blossomed"; the suffix *ra* is applied by the rule *namikampi-* (241), etc.
The statement "the lotuses bloom by the sun" [is used].
"Prācīm" means the eastern direction or the former state. "Kārpaṇyam" is the state of being a wretched person (miserliness).
Even though he has disregarded the salutations of other gods, [he acts] out of a prayer to Indra.
The meaning is that you are established in your own nature. //32//
He speaks with derision, saying "by speed," etc., to show that it is not only Indra who is distressed by you, but even Brahmā: "ārāddhum" means to worship;
"upanamati" means when he approaches; "apavyastaḥ" means agitated.

Because of the contradiction with swift movement. Therefore, "from their deeds" (*caritebhyaḥ*) means from the description of their deeds; "we do not restrain" (*na niyacchāmaḥ*) means we do not obstruct them, which here means we praise them. "Restraint" (*pratibandhaḥ*) means turning away;
thus, it is used in the sense of the ablative case (*apādāne*).
The fifth [case ending]: (242) *kimuta* = *kintu*; *sadhrīcīnām* = *sahāñcatīnām*.

The meaning is "of those who are similar"; by the rule *sahasya sadhriḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.95), the substitute *sadhri* occurs before the suffix *añc*. It surpasses = it transcends. Therefore, we shall restrain it.
This is the remainder [of the verse]. //33//
The progressive intensification of the great festivals consists in the sage’s arrival, his injunction, and the subsequent performance;
and this is expressed by the sixth case ending according to the rule *pūraṇa-ādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 2.2.11).
