Because of the very prohibition of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) when used with words having the sense of "filling" (*pūraṇa*), "satiety" (*suhita*), or "element" (*dhātu*), [the compound is not formed]; thus the meaning is "with great festivals. He states that very point with the words beginning "that which" (*yad*):
*upasthāna* means arrival; *atiprasaṅga* means excess, and that itself—
Regarding the musical performance (*saṅgītakam*): therein, the *nartakī* is the female dancer;
that is to say, she is overjoyed by the great honor occasioned by your arrival. Your command itself is a favor, for a dancer requires a commission to perform her dance.
Therefore, by the rule "spṛher īpsitaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.4.36), [the object of longing] receives the status of the recipient (*sampradāna*).
This means that the purpose of your coming must be stated.
[The address] "O son of Indumatī" (aindumateya).

The mention of birth in a divine field (*divyakṣetra*) is for the purpose of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*). Regarding the word "anyat" (another), the ellipsis is to be supplied as "due to the accomplishment of fame.
He states that this too is established with the words beginning with "nirmukta":
*nirmukta* means "without a bodice" (*niṣkañcuka*); Amara states: "One who is *nirmukta* is one whose bodice has been removed."
Acalendra is Mandara itself;
mantha is the churning-stick; by that means, he himself also—
*Saṃkṣubdhaḥ* means "equivalent to being thoroughly agitated"; the meaning is that, like one who is agitated, he churns the sides.
This is in the sense of the root *kṣubh* having the meaning of agitation.

It should be "kṣubhitam"; for it is said: "The word *kṣubdha* is used for a stirred drink (*mantha*), while *kṣubhitam* is used for anything else. How then is the form *kṣubdhā girinadī* ('the mountain river was agitated') justified? One must provide an explanation based on metaphorical comparison (*upamāna*).

*Kāśikā* (249): [The verse begins with] "tādṛśa-kṣīrasāgara-udara-gauraiḥ" and "bahulā-" etc. Regarding the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), it refers to the digits (*kalā*) which, due to the daily diminution of light, are as if melting away.

Because one experiences the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with an excellence of luminosity, there is a description of an excellence of brilliance for those very [rays]. Regarding the phrase "in the dark fortnight" (*bahulapakṣe*): in the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣe*), the moonlight follows immediately after the darkness.
The expression [is used] because it arises from a superior state (*parabhāga*). "The universe" (*viśvam*) refers to the three worlds (*jagattraya*);
"was beautified" (*aśobhi*) means it was illuminated. This is the *luṅ* (aorist) in the passive voice with the *ciṇ* suffix.

(250) Through this comparison of his fame to the serpent Śeṣa, the ocean of milk, and the moon—residing respectively in the three worlds beginning with Pātāla—the pervasion of the three worlds by his fame is established.
It has been indicated. //34//

Precisely because there is no other person to be enjoined who is equal to him, [the text] enjoins the acquisition of fame with intentional significance, beginning with "masses of fame" (*yaśastomān*).
Fame is the product born of giving.
Fame is born of valor; this is the convention of poets:
"Maturity is activity accompanied by enthusiasm."

"That action which, resulting in the successful fulfillment of what has been commenced, delights the entire universe is called *kīrti* (glory); if that very same [action] is produced by charity, it is designated as *yaśas* (fame). Thus says the *Bhāvaprakāśa*. (251) *Upacinu* = accumulate.

*Rasajñā* means the tongue; *cchiduraḥ* means "cut by itself," as in the case of one who is cut [by his own tongue] through its cleverness (*pāṇḍitya*). This is formed according to Pāṇini 3.2.162 (*vidibhidicchideḥ kurac*), which prescribes the suffix *-kurac* in the sense of the agent who is also the object (*karmakartṛ*). Such a person is [described].
"This is the abode" is an error—that is, delusion; the meaning is that through aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*), this delusion is destroyed. Or else, [it refers] to scholarship...
*Chiduraḥ* means "one who cuts" (*chedakaḥ*); [the suffix] *kurac* is used here in the sense of the agent (Pāṇini 3.1.135). The meaning is:

"bring about such fame that even the female *cakora* birds, though already acquainted with the essence of moonlight, drink it thinking, 'This is moonlight'"; for if one does not grant the requested Rāma, there will be ill-repute.
This is the intended meaning. It is a well-known convention among poets that fame is sweet;
as it was said by Śaṅkarācārya in his *Devīstuti*: "O Mother, for the cakora birds who drink together the mass of the moonlight of your fame, it becomes exceedingly sweet."
"Because their beaks are dull, those who have a distaste for sourness drink at will night after night the waves of nectar from the moon, mistaking them for sour gruel. (255) Moreover:

*Tejas* means majesty and splendor; *tamas* means darkness and calamity. Since friendship based on the occasion of a military expedition is liable to perish in its absence, let there be no pursuit for the sake of protecting it.

The meaning is "for the removal of darkness"; the intention is "produce such a radiance. By the use of the plural number in the word *tejobhiḥ* ("with radiances"), it is implied that they are endowed with radiance.
Rāma and others are indicated [by the term *rāma*].

*Tejas* is a specific element (*dhātuviśeṣa*); Amara states: "The white [element] is *tejas* and semen. And *tamasī* refers to the Rākṣasas who have that [darkness] as their primary quality; the singular number is used for the genus (*jātāvekavacanam*).
It is also suggested that the slaying of Rāvaṇa, for the sake of establishing the sovereignty of the Sun and others, can only be accomplished by Rāma and not by you. //35//

Having thus spoken for the benefit of Daśaratha, he introduces the main subject by means of stating his own purpose, beginning with "But... (*kiṃ tu*). Since the word *katipaya* signifies a part, the suffix *ac* is applied to the word *rātri* according to the rule *ahaḥsarvaikadeśa-* (Pāṇini 5.4.87); the accusative case is applied according to the rule *kālādhvanoḥ-* (Pāṇini 2.3.5). *Sadhrīcā* means accompanied (*sahitena*).

The sense is "for the purpose of battle. *Vitāna* means a sacrifice (*kratu*); as Amarasimha states: "The word *vitāna*, which is not feminine, denotes both a sacrifice and an expanse" (Amara-kośa 260). [This refers to] those who possess the restrictive rules associated with that [sacrifice]; for a *vrata* is indeed prescribed by the scriptures.
The rule (niyama):

"He shall be provided with a protector" means "let him quickly provide a protector. Because he is a great king, the expression is made indirect out of modesty (*vinaya*); it is used in the sense of a wish (*āśaṃsā*) regarding a swift action.
Or rather, the expression "Lord" (*nātha*) is used because of his sovereignty.
Avoiding the thought, "This shall be done by me alone; what is the need for Rāma?", he says:
"It is not only the protection of my sacrifice that must be performed by him, but rather—"

He confirms, by means of an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a different point), that the protection of subjects consists in both the preservation of the virtuous and the punishment of the wicked—beginning with the words "having placed in the middle," etc.
"Having placed in the middle" (*madhyekṛtya*) means having interposed; according to [Pāṇini 1.4.76]: "The word *madhya* is used in the sense of a 'position' (*pada*) and a 'pause' (*nivacana*)."
The suffix *lyap* is applied because it denotes a state of motion (*gatitvāt*). "She satisfies" means she pleases.
The meaning is that the boat for crossing the ocean [of existence] effects both the protection and the destruction of the world's darkness by means of the door that is dark-red like a cloud. By this—

The protection of the gods and the slaying of Rāvaṇa are indicated [here]. This is merely a designation for Rāma; the meaning is simply that you yourself are the protector. To the objection, "If this is so, what is the use of this internal excrescence? he says: "Such as this.
That which is beneficial to others, consisting in the manifestation of another, is not [superfluous].
The meaning is that it assists not only by way of its effect, but also by superimposing upon itself the status of being a benefactor.
"Having introduced some subject matter, [the statement] 'He should be known'— this is *arthāntaranyāsa*."
"The placement (nyāsa) of another object that is capable of accomplishing that [purpose]"—this is [the definition].
(265) Thus it is said. This...
The ornament called "Reason" (hetu); as it has been said: "That is designated as the Reason which illuminates the meaning of the probandum. //36//
Desiring to dispel the despondency of Daśaratha, which had been brought about by this very insistence,
he states his superiority over the lords of the earth, the upper regions, and the netherworlds in the verse beginning with "dṛṣṭa" (seen),
using a statement of contrast (*vyatireka*) that he was seen in person as the conqueror of the Asuras.

It has been stated that he was defeated by the Asuras; or alternatively, "he conquered like the Asuras," meaning he was a deceitful fighter. For it is said: "A conqueror is of two kinds: one who conquers through unrighteousness (Asura-vijayin) and one who conquers through righteousness (Dharma-vijayin)."
From the *Nītivākyāmṛta*:

(267) By the rule "when the agent is the object of comparison" (268), the suffix *ṇini* is applied. Or rather, it means that you yourself directly conquer the Asuras; for there is no one else capable [of this] other than yourself, O Rāma.

The meaning is that it does not exist. By this, Indra’s inconsistency has been stated. The "fish-logic" (mātsyanyāya) refers to the fact that the weak is oppressed by the strong; for such is the behavior among fish.
As it is said in the *Kāmandakīya*: "One fish devours another."
"Without doubt, a kinsman [honors] a kinsman; for the sake of destroying Rāvaṇa, Rāma honored Vibhīṣaṇa. (269) Thus.
That by which one is punished is *daṇḍa*—the fourth expedient (*upāya*); of that...

*Nītiḥ* means guidance (*nayanam*); *prayogaḥ* refers to the manner [of that guidance], with the word "that manner" being the ellipsis. By this, [the power] of Varuṇa [is indicated]. *Drāk* means quickly;
even at the mere utterance of the word "Pātāla," there is fear of the serpent (*ahi*), because of the abundance of such [serpents] therein.
Alternatively, there is the reading *pātālendrāt*; because he alone is a serpent (*sarpa*), there is fear [of him].
By the rule *bhītrārthānām* (Pāṇini 1.4.25), he functions as the *apādāna* (ablative).
Thus, "fear of the serpent" (*ahibhaya*) flashes forth as "fear arising from one's own side"; [and] "the fear of serpents for kings" (*mahībhujām ahibhayam*).

"‘Fear arising from one’s own side’ (svapakṣaprabhavaṃ bhayam)," according to Amara; by this [verse], [the fear] of Śeṣa [is indicated]. Thus, in every instance, there is a fault. "Tat" (that) begins the sentence.
"Naḥ" = of us, who are protected by you; by our merits (puṇyaiḥ), the earth (bhūḥ) shall be "rājanvatī" = possessed of a virtuous sovereign.

*Ajani* means "was born"; the *ciṇ* affix is used in the sense of the agent according to the rule *dīpajana* (Pāṇini 3.1.61). The meaning is that not only is there an absence of faults in you, but virtues also exist; for [the term] *rājanvān* applies to a land with a good king, and otherwise [it does not].
"Rājavān" is [defined] thus in the Amarakośa; "vīra" contains the reason for protection. //37//
The expression "svagata" (to himself) is used out of fear of the sages. Having thus determined that Rāma must necessarily be sent away, he says "How... and so forth.
*Śaṅku* means a dart or thorn. The word *pāda* denotes honor; [it is used] at the end of a name...
According to the statement in the *Amaraśeṣa*, "The word *caraṇa* is to be understood as meaning 'feet' (*pāda*) when denoting those worthy of worship. (274) Thus,
through the two words *śītala-pāda*, the sage's nature as the moon is made manifest.
The particle *api* is used here in the sense of conceiving what was previously inconceivable. The construction is: "It will arise;
how will it arise?"—namely, "How has he, who is the source of all bliss, become the cause of my suffering?"

He weakens the doubt by means of an illustration, beginning with "Or it is seen," and so forth. *Kandalīs* are sprouts. *Aṅkasthāna* is a place of reproach. This is the ornament known as *nidarśana*; as it has been said: "The illustration (*nidarśana*)..."
"The proclamation of well-known meanings serves to cut through doubt" (275).
Since the very avoidance [of doubt] is the means, he says "Kūrmarāja," etc.
"Gotragrāvāṇaḥ" refers to the kulaparvatas (principal mountain ranges); "grāvāṇau" [refers to two mountains].
"Śaila and pāṣāṇa mean 'stone'," according to Amara. *Ekadhurīṇa* means "one who bears that which is a single burden (*ekā* = equal, *dhūḥ* = burden)";
the suffix *kha* is applied here by the rule *ekadhurālluk ca*. All [these], beginning with the tortoise, are...
The sense is that the Raghu dynasty alone bears as much of a burden as all [the others] combined, because of its disposition toward generosity; and it has been said:
"By cows, by Brahmins, by the Vedas, by virtuous women, and by speakers of truth..."

"The earth is sustained by seven [kinds of people]: those who are free from greed and those whose nature is generosity. (278) Thus [it is said]. "Me" refers to one who does not give when requested. "Censured" means reviled.

*Vaimukhyāt* means "out of aversion"; *nindā* (reproach) occurs in the sense of the imperative (*loṭ*) when considering what ought to be done, meaning "let it be so. The thought is: "May I become a defiler of the family. *Ha* expresses grief;
the defilement of the family is caused by one's own single transgression.
And there is the figurative expression of aversion, just as one says "the cloth" even when only a single part of the cloth has been burnt; such is the intended meaning. //38//
Having observed the despair of Daśaratha caused by the sense of "mine-ness," and loosening his attachment by means of an illustration, he says: "O Royal Sage! and so forth.
Furthermore, a sage is not attached.

This is the meaning. *Mamakāra* means the act of forming the conceit "mine"; the particle *mama* is used in the sense of the conceit of ownership, and its *kāra*—the suffix *-kāra*—denotes the verbal expression of that state of "belonging to me."
Or rather, it is the utterance [of the word]; the enjoyment is caused by the prince;
in this case, the effort belongs to one, while the fruit belongs to another.
He provides an illustration, beginning with "kaṣṭa" and so forth.
*Vedhavyathā* is the pain arising from being pierced by a needle. *Kaṣṭaḥ* means unbearable.
There is exhaustion (*klama*) in carrying [the weight], [which affects] the ears; however, as for the earring (*kuṇḍala*), [it does not].
The ornament of the cheek. //39//
By "Your Honor" (tatrabhavatā), it is meant by you, the venerable one;
"thus" (evam) refers to the statement that Rāma is to be enjoyed by the subjects;
"being esteemed" (sambhāvyamānāḥ) means being highly honored.
*Akṛtāstraḥ* means one who has not been trained in the use of weapons.
*Kṣīrakaṇṭhaḥ* means one whose throat is filled with milk; because he has always been suckled at the breast, he is not qualified [for martial training]; the meaning is that he is a very young child.
"Stupefied" means devoid of discernment; the word "in sending" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
He says "O friend," and so forth, with a touch of irony, because the first two [reasons] are for the most part unproven.
"Having placed before him" means having set him in front, or having appointed him as a domestic priest (*purohita*).
The *brahmacaryavratas* are the Vedic observances; *brahman* is the Veda, and its *carya* is the study [of it], as well as its auxiliary rites:
those dedicated to Prajāpati, Soma, Agni, and Viśvedevas.

These consist of the *upākarma* (commencement) and *utsarjana* (conclusion) rites, which are ancillaries to the study of the four sections beginning with the *prājāpatya*. By this, the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*) becomes complete; as it was stated by Yājñavalkya: "Having brought the Veda, or the vows, or indeed both, to completion, one whose studentship has remained unviolated..."
"One should marry a woman endowed with auspicious marks. (280) By this, the study of the primary Vedas is indicated.

The consecrations of the science of archery (*dhanurveda*) consist of the initiation for the purpose of receiving the mantras of the missiles of Indra, Varuṇa, and Agni, as well as the employment and withdrawal of those missiles.
There was a certain Prajāpati named Kṛśāśva, from whom Viśvāmitra studied the science of archery (dhanurveda).
"They depend upon us" means they become subject to us; this is used in the sense of a locative of sphere (*vaiṣayika-adhikaraṇe*).
The seventh [case]; (282) according to Amara, "adhīnaḥ, nighnaḥ, āyattaḥ" mean dependent.
Regarding the word "tāvat": first comes the instruction in the science of archery (dhanurveda), and afterwards [the preparation] for battle.

The meaning is "the act of enjoining. "Out of favor" (*prasādāt*) is an expression of devotion to the teacher. "Restraint of humility" (*vinayoparodhaḥ*) is the internal suppression of the mind brought about by humility.
"Exhaled breath" (*ucchvasitam*) means life.
*rājabījāḥ* means those belonging to the royal lineage; according to Amarasimha, *rājabījo rājavaṃśyaḥ*. *Sampradāyaḥ* means acquisition through traditional succession.

Regarding *parivatsarān*: the accusative case is used according to the rule *kālādhvanoratyantasaṃyoge* (Pāṇini 2.3.5). *Upaniṣad* means a secret or esoteric teaching. *Adhyagīṣṭhāḥ* means you have studied.
*Asambhāvanayā* means with disregard; the sense is: "enough [of that]," meaning let it not be so.
The darkness itself is the *tiraskariṇī* (curtain), because it acts as a veil;
even though it is "minuter" (*aṇutara*), meaning it has only slightly arisen.
By means of the analogy of the sun and darkness, his status as the direct enemy of the Daityas [is established].
It indicates:
"tādṛśī talinā" means "so light"; the *Viśva* lexicon states, "talinā means sparse and light. (286) "Adharottareṇa" means by way of a reply, [that is,] with a response. Of the subsequent...
The meaning is that she is not even capable of giving a reply. "Apart" (*apavārya*); the word "the sage" (*ṛṣim*) is to be supplied as the object.
Regarding this, Bharata states: "'A secret is told to another by turning away [from others]—this is called *apavārita*. (287)
"Rāma speaks thus, saying 'he should be sent'; the remainder of the sense is 'what should be done?
This is for the sake of discerning the facial expression of the king, who asks while doubting regarding the matter of giving."
Having resolved upon the gift, he expresses his consent for the donation with the words beginning "O Kauśika," and so forth.

The underlying meaning is that, after due consideration of the beggar, the donor, the purpose, and the object of the request, a refusal is not appropriate. By saying "we give our consent," [he indicates] Rāma's well-being.
And he said: //40//
He confirms that this alone is what is called the happiness of sovereignty by means of the verse beginning with "jagati" and so forth. *Bhāraḥ* means maintenance (*bharaṇam*).
*Yathākāmam* means that which has been obtained without transgressing one's desires.
*Sampattiḥ* means *sampat*; it is an avyayībhāva compound according to the rule *yathāsādṛśye* (Pāṇini 2.1.7).
He says "and especially" because by not doing this, there would be a transgression of the Guru's command;
[he says] "in order to fulfill," etc.,
under the pretext of fulfilling the desires and messages of those who seek them.
The meaning is that he commanded precisely the dispatching of Rāmabhadra; by the phrase "by the family preceptor," he expresses that his word was not to be transgressed. //42//
He restates the very vision of samādhi along with its logical justification, beginning with "consisting of meditation" (dhyānamaya), and so forth. *Niṣṭhā* means a vow (*vrata*);
those who practice by means of it are called *naiṣṭhikas*.

The suffix *ṭhak* is applied [to the root] *carati* (289); [the term] *niṣṭhā* [is used] in the sense of excellence, established state, destruction, end, religious observance (*vrata*), and request (*yācñā*) (290).
Vaijayantī;
it is so called because it pervades all paths, according to [Pāṇini 5.2.7]:
*tatsarvādeḥ*.
By such [statements], "kha" is established. *Mati* means knowledge. Regarding objects (*viṣayeṣu*), such as form and so forth:
what is called *dhyāna* is a stream of homogeneous cognitions (*sajātīyapratyayapravāha*) not interspersed with heterogeneous cognitions (*vijātīyapratyaya*).

The meaning is that the mental modifications (*vṛttis*) consist of transformations of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) characterized by one-pointedness; "consisting of that" (*tanmayī*) means "abounding in that," according to the rule *tatprakṛtavacane mayaṭ* (Pāṇini 5.4.21), which signifies being preponderantly composed of that. "Preponderance" refers to the state of being primarily constituted by that.

The *Kāśikā* states "being the subject under discussion" (293); that is to say, the very nature of meditation (*dhyāna*). The "falling" (*pāta*) of that "vision" (*dṛṣṭi*), which is the eye, refers to its connection with sense objects;
by means of that [connection], [the objects], though existing, are as if non-existent because they do not act as an obstruction.

When there exist those [objects] for which there is remoteness caused by time and space, immediately after that, the all-pervading intellect—meaning consciousness—proceeds, that is, it moves forward without obstruction;
according to the rule: "The root *kram* is used in the senses of activity (*vṛtti*), creation (*sarga*), and extension (*tāyana*). (Pāṇini 1.3.38).
Regarding the term *vṛtti*, the *ātmanepada* [suffix] is applied;
the *Kāśikā* states that "vṛtti" means "absence of obstruction.
Upon the removal of the obscuring factor by means of this *vṛtti*.

The consciousness delimited by that [internal organ] perceives the object, just as the eye perceives form when darkness has been dispelled by lamps and the like; such is the process [of perception], [occurring] through the power of the sovereignty born of yoga. (296)
The meaning is that even a collection of objects separated by space and time appears as if present before one's eyes and as if connected to the present moment. //43//
He states the refutation regarding the opposing view (vipakṣe bādhakam) with the words beginning "of actions" (*kriyāṇām*).

"Action" (*kriyā*) refers to sacrifice (*yāga*). "Having approached" (*upasthāya*) means having reached. "The Blessed One" (*bhagavatī*) is an expression used by virtue of her power. "Houses" (*gṛhān*) refers to stages of life (*āśramān*); [as it is said: "the word *gṛhāḥ* is masculine..."
And according to Amara, [the word *bhūman*] refers specifically to abundance. From "kleśāt" means from exhaustion.
The word "vā" is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). It is merely a story; how much more so [is it true]?

The word "only" (eva) has the sense of "the family. The intention is that the destruction of the family would occur due to the agitation caused by a great man; therefore, he should be sent away. //44//
Revealing his approval by way of granting Rāmabhadra himself, he says:

"If you," and so forth. If even you, who are the sustainer of Brahmā and the other gods, require Rāma for the protection of the sacrifice, then [he must go], because he is the sustainer of all the worlds.
The meaning is that we ourselves are the lords of the earth.
This begins from here and extends up to the words: "Whatever is pleasing to you and to our father" (298).

The *parinyāsa* (development) is the structural element (*aṅga*) because the seed (*bīja*), which consists of Rāma’s resolve, is directed toward its fruition through his acceptance of the expedition for the sake of the battle with the Rākṣasas; as it has been said: "Its [the seed's] accomplishment..."
Regarding the term "pariṇyāsa" (299): the "accomplishment" (*niṣpatti*) of that seed is its state of having sprouted. //45//
"Who is here?"—the change to *s* occurs because it belongs to the *kaska*-class; "exists" is the ellipsis.
Because of its connection with the word *antareṇa*, the word *prakāśam* takes the accusative case according to the rule *antarāntareṇa yukte*. *Antareṇa* means "without. *Ujjihīte* means "rises up."

"Surādhīśa," and so forth. "Aparathā" means otherwise (*anyathā*); [it is formed] by the rule *thāl* used in the sense of manner (*prakāravacane*). "To create" (*kartum*) means to fashion (*nirmātum*).
"Others" (*apare*) means those other than those created by Brahmā.
The ancient Brahmās—acting as representatives of the primordial creators, the Seven Sages such as Marīci and others; the fathers of the worlds, that is, their creators;
and the Seven Sages—and by the word "ca" (and), the constellations as well. Their satisfaction...
At the request of Brahmā and others, the path known as Vaiśvānarapatha— located to the south of Agastya’s hermitage and to the north of the Lokāloka mountain peak,
consisting of the paths of the twenty-seven lunar mansions, each individually— [was established].
In the midst of the threefold division known as the northern Vaiśvānara, the southern Dakṣiṇa, and the [western] Irāvatā, which consists of the three paths (vīthīs).
The southern path; as it is stated in the Vāyu Purāṇa: "The middle station is Jāradgava."
"Likewise, Airāvata is in the north; Vaiśvānara is designated here in truth as being in the south.
(303) In this regard—the three southern paths follow the sequence ending in the north.
The path of Aja, the path of Mṛga, and the path of Vaiśvānara;
the triad of middle paths consisting of the path of Ṛṣabha, the path of Go,
and the path of Jāradgava.
The three northern paths are Airāvata-vīthī, Nāga-vīthī,
and Gaja-vīthī; beyond those is the path known as Pitṛyāṇa.
The path:
(304) they are "dhṛtāḥ," meaning established; as it is said in that very same place: "That which is north of Agastya and south of the Ajavīthī is the Pitṛyāṇa."
That indeed is the path outside the path of Vaiśvānara.
The great-souled sages who maintain the sacred fires dwell there;
that is the path for those who undertake [the rites] out of a desire for the worlds.
The Dakṣiṇas, O Brahmā, establish your movement again in age after age through continuity, austerity,
boundaries, and ritual action; thus do they revolve.
"They remain until the dissolution of all beings, having resorted to the southern path of the Sun as long as the moon and stars exist"—
thus is the ancient narrative concerning his life.
Pertaining to the *Rāmāyaṇa*, it "makes known" = proclaims;
as it is stated in the *Rāmāyaṇa*: "Creating again another set of Seven Sages situated on the southern path..."
Overwhelmed with rage, he created another garland of stars. (306) Thus [ends the verse]. 46.

In the phrase "so 'pi," the particle *api* expresses possibility (*sambhāvanā*). Regarding "himself" (*svayam*): the meaning is that Viśvāmitra alone will act [as the officiant], and not some person belonging to him. "How can this be? expresses astonishment (*āścarya*).

The form *viśvāmittra* is used figuratively [to denote the person]. In expressions such as "this one, this one," when there is agitation caused by intense regard, there is either a reduplication of the word *ayam* itself, or two instances of the substitute *ayaṃ*;
for it is said that "in cases of haste, there are two [forms]."
Because of the statement "it should be said" (vaktavyam); and according to the *Kāśikā*, "restlessness is activity caused by agitation.
Such [is it] = incomparable. [The word] *bhayaṅkarīḥ* [is used] in the sense of "fear," as in the rule for *megha-ṛti-bhayeṣu*.
By the rule *kṛñaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.56), the suffix *khac* is applied; the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is to be considered. How so?

This is used in the sense of wonder (*āścarya*), meaning "this is improbable. "This" refers to the ferocity of one who is peaceful. It is indeed established; the meaning is that it exists in other cases as well. It flashes forth in darkness—that is, in physical gloom and in the quality of *tamas*. //47//

They marvel, that is, they perform an act of wonder; [this is derived] from the root *citraṅ* meaning "wonder" with the suffix *kyac* according to the rules *citraṅ āścarye* (Pāṇini 3.1.17) and *namovarivaḥ...* (Pāṇini 3.1.19).
Regarding "vratetyādi":
*vihatikarībhiḥ* means those whose nature is to strike down (*vihananaśīlābhiḥ*); [this is derived] by [Pāṇini 3.2.20] *kṛño hetutācchīlyānulaomyeṣu*. (312)

By the rule *ityādinā* [Pāṇini 3.2.134], the suffix *ṭa* is applied in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*), and by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added. *Gṛṇanti* means "they speak. Regarding *namat* and so forth:
this statement is made because [the sun] destroys darkness through its brilliance (*tejas*). //48//
"Brahman," and so forth.

"Of the vivarta of the Brahman-light" means of that which consists of a false transformation (mithyā-pariṇāma); the meaning is that the Vedic light itself appears in the form of the sacrificial vessel (caru).
Rāma is the first part, because it is well known that Rāma and the others originated from the first and other parts. (314)

*Āraṇyakāḥ* refers to humans born in the forest (*araṇya*); the suffix *vuñ* is applied according to the rule *araṇyānmanuṣye* (Pāṇini 4.2.129). *Kim api* means "inexpressible. [The phrase] "not merely," and so forth, [is used].

"By [the word] 'vatsaiḥ' (by the calves)," this is an expression of affection (*vātsalya*). The meaning is that by his own birth and by his religious observances, he made both Vibhāṇḍaka and Daśaratha possessors of sons. (316)

"Those who [worship] Maitrāvaruṇi," and so forth. "Purohitayataḥ" means "one who appoints a domestic priest" (*purohitaṃ kurvataḥ*). In the reading *purohitavataḥ*, it means "one who has placed [a priest] at the head";
the suffix *ktavatu* (according to Pāṇini 3.2.102) replaces the root *dhā* with *hi* (according to Pāṇini 7.4.42). "Jajñire" means "were born."

*Vainayikīḥ*: *Vinaya* means mastery over the senses; those [disciplines] for which this is the purpose are so called. [The suffix] *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule "prayojanam" (Pāṇini 5.1.109). *Te* means yours; *eṣa* refers to Daśaratha; *añcala* means the last [part], as in "the *añcala* placed on the back" (*kakṣyā pṛṣṭhe kṛto'ñcalaḥ*), referring to the edge of a garment.
"Tvaccalo vastiḥ" (the bladder moves with you), according to the *Vaijayantī*; or "eṣate" may be a single word, meaning "he reaches," from the root "eṣṛ/preṣṛ" in the sense of "going."
Thus is the etymological root (dhātu). These [beings] beginning with Rāma possess sovereignty through austerity;
the meaning is that they have obtained it by the power of austerity. //50//
"Sāvitrau" means "the two whose lord is Savitṛ.
"May you be long-lived" expresses a wish for longevity in order to avoid the reproach of Daśaratha.
"To himself" refers to the supreme sovereignty residing in Rāma.
Because it must be kept secret for the sake of following the ways of the world;
"Vasiṣṭha," etc.; *ābhyudayikīm* means having prosperity as its purpose; *kulīnāḥ* means those born of noble lineage.
"From the family to the sky" (322). He states the reason for this [statement] with the second half [of the verse]:
*vārī* means a post for tying an elephant, according to Amarasimha’s lexicon (*vārī tu gajabandhanī*);
there, the lord of elephants was bound.
She is eternally the water [of life] for the God, never departing from his two breasts;
by her parts— that is, by her portions— she herself dwells there, so the sense is to be understood.

By stating that [the moon] dwells here even while sporting upon the breasts of Lakṣmī, the text indicates the Lord of Śrī’s (Viṣṇu’s) special fondness for the solar dynasty through his attachment to those breasts; furthermore,
by mentioning the birth of Rāma, the presence of Lakṣmī within this lineage is also affirmed.
The meaning is that the fact that the Raghu dynasty became the sustenance for all the world was obtained through the power of Vasiṣṭha. //51//
Regarding the phrase "the conduct of the learned" (*śiṣṭācāra*), he praises the Lord through direct perception with the words beginning with "you" (*tvam*) and so forth.
The term *daśatayīḥ* refers to those consisting of ten maṇḍalas as their constituent parts; [this is derived] by the rule: "The suffix *tayap* is added to a numeral to denote a part. (Pāṇini 5.2.42).

The suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15). The term "Ṛc" is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all the Vedas. By stating "he remembered," he asserts its eternity through the exclusion of [the notion of] creation. The sacrificial fire is indeed the *tretā*.

The term *tretā* is derived from the three designations, such as the *āhavanīya* fire and so forth; it is grammatically correct by virtue of belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group (Pāṇini 6.3.109), meaning "this triad of fires is the *tretā*."
Thus says Amara; the word *agni* is used here as in the case of a young elephant (*karikalabha*).
(328) *Svāhākāram* means having uttered the word *svāhā*; [this is according to the rule] "and in the second case" (Pāṇini 5.4.48). (329)
Thus ends the section on the *ṇamul* suffix. Regarding the phrase "the oblation offered by the sacrificers for your pleasure," he sips it—that is, he consumes it—according to the rule:
*ṣṭhivuklamvācamāṃ śiti* (Pāṇini 7.3.75).

Long. Here, "water" means milk; [the term] *kṣīrodajaleśaya* (lying in the water of the milk-ocean) [is formed] with the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case according to *Pāṇini 6.3.18*: *śayavāsavāsiṣvakālāt*.
[The term] *kratuliha* (licking the sacrifice).
This is a statement containing the reason for the introduction [of the topic]. "Nigrāhitāraḥ" means "they will be defeated," using the periphrastic future (*luṭ*).
(52) (332) The ellipsis to be supplied is: "We shall do whatever is pleasing to you. [The word] "bhavataḥ" [means "to you"].

The mention of Vāmadeva first is for the purpose of indicating the preeminence of the family priest; his status as the recipient (*sampradāna*) is established by the rule *ruccarthānām* (Pāṇini 1.4.33);
this is an elliptical expression.

Because of the force of suffering, there is an inability to speak; and suffering arises from the contemplation of giving. *Manyoḥ* means of grief (*śoka*); *utpīḍaḥ* means its intensification. The word "throat" (*kaṇṭha*) is used figuratively to refer to the tone of voice.
He looked toward the face of Vāmadeva in order to receive the instruction for pronouncing the remaining portion: "These two are your Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa."

The auspicious nature of the sound of a conch is established because it is stated in the section on military expeditions: "Elephants, horses, kettledrums, conchs, pairs of birds, courtesans, full vases, and banners [are auspicious]. (334)
From this point up to "This moon is the kinsman of the night-lotus" (335),
there is the dramatic element named *vilobhana* (enticement), consisting of the description of the virtues of Daśaratha and others.
As it has been said: "The proclamation of virtues is seduction" (336).
The auspicious omen is the statement that the midday twilight brings happiness, as well as the mention of the *abhijit* muhūrta; this [is for] his departure for the sake of victory.

Because it is praiseworthy. On this point, the *Lalla-saṃhitā* states: "That eighth muhūrta which is designated by the name Viriñci and is called Abhijit—having abandoned the southern [quarter] during that time, [one should act] elsewhere."
"For one who has departed, there is the attainment of victory. (337) Now, it should be understood that the hermitage of Siddha is situated on the slope [of the mountain].
Regarding the verse beginning with "kirati" and so forth: *mihiraḥ* means the sun.
"Mihira, aruṇa, and pūṣan" (Amara-kośa 1.3.35). *Viṣvadrīcaḥ* means "pervading all directions";
the substitution of *adri* [for *viṣvak*] occurs according to the rule beginning with "viṣvag-devayoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.3.92). For this very reason...
"Like a land-tortoise" means equal to a land-tortoise; "it moves" means it contracts.
For a tortoise contracts on land due to its dwelling in water.
"With motes of dust" means with particles. [The reason is] that there is water at the tip of the trunk.
This is the established usage. *Masṛṇām* means smooth or glossy, because of its moisture. [*Kacchasthalīm*;
*kacchaḥ* means a watery region; [this is formed] by [the rule] *adhiśīṅ* (Pāṇini 1.4.46), etc.

The state of being an object [is expressed]; "lying down" [is so called] because of the inability to endure burning; and that [inability] is indicated by the word "even" (*api*), which signifies a requirement even when there is only slight coldness. //53//
*Paṭīra* is a sandalwood tree (*candanataru*); its hollow (*koṭara*) itself is the *kuṭīra*, a small hut.
The suffix *ra* is applied according to the rule: "The suffix *ra* is added after *kuṭī*, *śamī*, and *śuṇḍā*" (Pāṇini 5.3.88).
"Pratyakṣara... and so forth. *Sudhā* is a specific kind of nectar to be drunk by serpents;
as it has been said: "May this very *sudhā* be the medicine for the kings of the *nāgas*."
"Vaḥ" (342). For this very reason, there is the state of being "poisonless" (*nirviṣatva*) regarding the *āśis*—that is, the fangs;
for Amara states: "The word *āśis* [is used] in the sense of a serpent's fang. (343)

"Bhogas" means hoods; as Amarasimha states: "The word *bhoga* denotes pleasure, the maintenance of women and so forth, and the hood or body [of a serpent]. Its state of being exceedingly adorned is due to its beautiful configuration and its freedom from the defect of protruding fangs.

With their joy, perspiration, and horripilation covered by a bodice—meaning a sloughed-off skin—their hair stood on end and they broke into sweat; regarding "horripilation," Amara states: *romāñco romaharṣaṇam* (345). //54//

"Slow," and so forth. "Trembling and slowness" [result] from the weight of the jewels and from being overcome by the liquid [mercury]. Regarding the word "with their heads" (*śirobhiḥ*): the instrumental case is used according to Pāṇini 2.3.21, *itthambhūtalakṣaṇe*.

"Prāuḍhāḥ" means possessing firmness, and for that very reason, they possess the nature of staffs; by them, "sphāyadbhyaḥ" means from those that are increasing; "sandhibhyaḥ" means from the joints; "prasarantaḥ" means spreading forth, not leaking away.
And those whose streams of sweat caused by joy were uninterrupted due to the absence of any gaps;
the irregularity in the pronunciation of syllables was due to the possession of two tongues.
The quality of being delightful arises from the absence of indistinctness in the syllables.
Although the two verses have the same meaning, there is no tautology because they constitute a statement of assent. //55//

The modesty [shown] was out of respect for the King; the embarrassment arose from being separated from the Prince; and the smile was intended to manifest his graciousness as a sign that the purpose he wished to express had been accomplished. What is called *dīkṣā* occurs immediately after the *dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi* sacrifice.
The specific observance consisting of wearing the black antelope skin and so forth must be undertaken; for that purpose,
one enters the sacrificial ground.
"‘We have come to this place of sacrifice on earth,’ [with these words] he settles upon the sacrificial ground (devayajana)," so says the Sūtra.
*Adhyavasāna* means entry (*praveśa*); by metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it refers to the time of entry. *Tat* (that) refers to the cause. *Madhurā* means dear (*priyā*);
*goṣṭhī* means an assembly (*samāja*). As it is said: "A gathering, a council, or a social circle (*goṣṭhī*)" (Amara-kośa 2.7.349).
Thus says Amara: since the mutual proximity of father and son is a source of affection,
those who are *niṣṭhurāḥ*— meaning lacking in courtesy— in causing its *bhaṅge*, that is, their separation, are *prathame*, meaning they are the foremost [in such cruelty].

The designation *sarvanāman* (pronoun) is established by the first sūtra (Pāṇini 1.1.27). The meaning of the word "first" (*prathama*) is that although this [sūtra] appears harsh at first glance, it becomes sweet in its ultimate result; for this very reason, the expression "we desire" (*icchāmaḥ*) is used.

Vāmadeva’s agitation arises from the completion of the sentence "O Kauśika, depart," by supplying the remainder of the speech intended by Daśaratha— which was interrupted by an incomplete utterance caused by grief regarding the departure of the sage with the prince.
It is for the purpose of accomplishing the state of having auspicious signs (*sunimittatā*). Perform it; go! The verbal root is *sādhṛ* in the sense of "going" (Dhātupāṭha 351).
[He will cause] Kauśika to suffer; he will cause him pain, that is, in an adverse manner.
He will cause [her] to do so; by the rule "after *duḥkha*, when used in the sense of opposition," the suffix *ḍāc* is applied;
the meaning is that he will cause her mind to be afflicted by his own mental derangement.
The meaning is that he will act against himself;
he causes suffering through his own inconsistency.
Regarding this, the *Kāśikā* states: "Adversity is the affliction of the mind of one who is being propitiated. (353)
“Viṣayāḥ” means countries. The word “vā” is used for emphasis. “Sukhayiṣyati” means he will make [them] happy; this is the sense. //56//
"We" is an indication of what belongs to the self (*ātmiya*), while "Kauśika" is an indication of what does not belong to the self (*anātmiya*). [The thought is:
"These indeed belong to the self, they do not belong to the non-self," and "These indeed do not belong to the self, they do not belong to the self."
The division of categories— the division of objects— consists in the thought "these are not mine" and "these indeed are mine"; the meaning is that it is the cognition of difference.

The sense is that he feels affection toward everyone. Because both the Sage, who is affectionate without cause, and the sweet Rāmabhadra are pure, there is affection even in the absence of external causes such as fatherhood and so forth.
It indeed happens, as in the case of the moon and the night-lotus; thus he says, "That which [belongs] to the moon," and so forth. "Calamity or prosperity" refers to setting and rising;
"sorrow and joy" also flash forth; and "it follows" means that it itself undergoes waning and waxing.
Regarding the statement "he resorts to [it]," in that sense, *jani* means origination;
its agent (*tatkartā*) is the one being born (*jāyamāna*); his state of being the material cause (*prakṛtitā*) is his state of being the father (*pitṛtā*).
...as far as this condition is the cause, it prevails: "Pronouns bring about the identity between that which is being pointed out and that which is being referred back."

"They assume those respective genders by way of grammatical turn" (354); thus, the masculine designation "this" (*ayam*) is used with reference to the word *upādhi*. [The phrase] "it imitates that" (*tasya anuharate*) means it emulates it;
the ellipsis is to be supplied as "its misfortune or its prosperity."

Because of the substitution of *ñit* [for *nit*], the *ātmanepada* ending is used. As in the example, "His mind was drawn away even more," the term functions as an imitation due to the influence of the prefix (*upasarga*). Alternatively, the meaning is: "He imitates that" (*tasyānuharate*), which is to say, he becomes equal to it; for "imitation" (*anuharaṇa*) means acting with equality, by means of that.
The genitive case [is used] by the phrase "tulyārtha" (having the same meaning),
as in the expression "the son resembles the father."

The meaning is that there is contraction and expansion of a luster equal to the moon. As for the phrase "what is this connection?"—it means what is its basis? The meaning is that there is no external connection whatsoever.
"Anabhisandhi" means without condition (*anupādhi*); "praṇaya" means friendship (*sauhṛda*), [referring to] those who possess it.
They were addressed in that manner; for the Viśvaprakāśa states: "The word *praṇaya* may mean acquaintance, a request, or even friendship. (358)//57//
Having raised the doubt that there might be a relationship such as that of progenitor and offspring between the moon and the night-lily,
and having determined that other factors such as a biological father are involved,
[the author] repeats the words of Vāmadeva— "O mine of jewels," and so forth— stating: "Let it be said that the night-lily is the father of the moon."
What? It is that mine of jewels (ratnākara). What is meant by "the group of siblings"?
They are Amṛta and the others. Nevertheless, the ellipsis is "he feels affection for them."
Or rather—his father was Ratnākara, and his brothers were Amṛta and the others. What more need be said? It is impossible to mention their names all at once.
This is the meaning; for this very reason, the designation "mine of jewels" (*ratnākara*) and so forth was employed.

By those [qualities] such as fatherhood and the like—which are not [intrinsic] causes—the remainder is "in affectionateness"; what is the purpose? It is that which is expressed by the phrase, "the moon is the friend of the night-lotus."

In this context, "another reality" (*tattvāntara*) means a specific, determined cause that is indeed something else; the meaning is that there exists nothing external [to it]; [the phrase] "in a distinction or on an occasion" refers to an *antara*.
Thus says Amara (359):
"That is inconceivable" means it does not become an object of thought; how much less, then, an object of speech—this is the meaning. On this point, Bhavabhūti says: "It interweaves..."
"There is indeed no other cause for things than this; for affections do not depend upon external conditions. (360) //58//
By the words "Let us console Queen Kausalyā," he indicates that she possesses affection for Lakṣmaṇa as well as for Rāma.
"All have exited" refers to those whose single-day performance consists of a unified plot.
"The hero is present;
the act [ends] with three or four characters, at the conclusion of which there is his exit," as it has been stated. (361)

Regarding the term "Aṅka" (Act): its status as an act is due to its consisting of the direct representation of the conduct of the characters, and because it comprises the prince's journey uninterrupted by the description of his friendship with virtuous men.

Furthermore, because of the repeated connection of the subject matter and because it serves as the locus for the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) arising from the arrangement of various types of meanings, it has been said: "An act (*aṅka*) is that which is performed by a hero visible to the audience and is preceded by the manifestation of the *bindu*."
It is the locus of the aesthetic flavor (rasa) derived from the arrangement of various kinds of meanings.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Anargharāghava-pañcikā* composed by Śrī Viṣṇubhaṭṭa. (362)
